content.title: Evaluation
content.explanation:
Your model finished training! But is it actually good? AI models require specialized evaluation metrics.

**Lexical Metrics (Old School):**
• **BLEU:** Measures exact word overlap between the AI's output and a human reference. Great for translation, terrible for creative writing.
• **ROUGE:** Measures recall (how much of the human reference was captured by the AI). Often used for summarization.

**Semantic Metrics (Modern):**
• **BERTScore:** Uses a neural network to measure the *meaning* similarity between sentences. Even if the AI uses completely different words, it gets a high score if the meaning matches the human reference.

**LLM-as-a-Judge:**
The most modern and reliable automated technique. You write a prompt for GPT-4 instructing it to act as a judge. You feed it your fine-tuned model's output and ask GPT-4 to grade it on a scale of 1-10 based on helpfulness, tone, and accuracy.

content.title: Expert Concept: The Danger of Overfitting
content.explanation:
Evaluation metrics only matter if your model isn't broken. If you train for too many epochs, your model will 'Overfit'.

Overfitting means the model literally memorized the training data word-for-word, but entirely lost its ability to generalize to new questions. It becomes a glorified database instead of an intelligent AI.

**How to spot it:**
During training, you track two lines: **Training Loss** and **Validation Loss**.
Training loss always goes down. But if Validation Loss starts going up, STOP the training immediately. You have started overfitting.

content.title: Reading Loss Curves
content.explanation: The bright red spike is every ML Engineer's worst nightmare. While the blue line (training loss) decreases, the red line (validation loss) aggressively spiking upwards indicates that the model has begun catastrophically overfitting.

content.title: Choosing the Right Metric
content.description: You fine-tuned a model to write highly creative marketing copy. Which evaluation method should you rely on?

choices.text: BLEU Score
choices.outcome: Incorrect. BLEU checks for exact word matches. Creative marketing copy rarely uses exact word matches.

choices.text: LLM-as-a-Judge (using GPT-4)
choices.outcome: Correct! A powerful LLM can judge nuance, creativity, and brand tone much better than traditional word-overlap metrics.

content.title: What is LangChain?
content.explanation: Before we write any code, let's understand WHY LangChain exists and what problem it solves. If you've ever called the OpenAI API directly, you know it works — but what happens when your app grows?

content.title: The Problem Without LangChain
content.body: Imagine you build a chatbot using the OpenAI API. It works great! But then your boss says: 'Can we also support Claude and Gemini?' Now you need to rewrite your code for 3 different APIs, each with different formats. That's the problem LangChain solves.

content.title: LangChain = Universal Adapter
content.body: LangChain is a Python framework that gives you ONE consistent way to talk to ANY LLM. Write your code once, then swap between GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, or Llama by changing a single line. Your entire app logic stays exactly the same.

content.title: Think of it Like a Power Strip
content.body: Different countries have different power outlets. A universal adapter lets you plug in anywhere. LangChain is that adapter for LLMs — it standardizes the 'plug' so your app works with any AI provider.

content.title: Beyond Just Calling LLMs
content.body:
LangChain isn't just about calling models. It provides building blocks for:

- Prompt Templates — reusable prompt designs
- Output Parsers — get clean JSON instead of messy text
- Chains — connect multiple steps into a pipeline
- Memory — make your chatbot remember conversations
- Tools — let LLMs search the web, run code, etc.

content.title: The 'Lego Blocks' Philosophy
content.body: Each LangChain component is like a Lego block. A `PromptTemplate` is one block. A `ChatModel` is another. An OutputParser is another. You snap them together to build whatever you want — from a simple Q&A bot to a complex multi-agent system.

content.title: When to Use LangChain
content.body:
Use LangChain when you need:

✅ Multi-provider support (OpenAI + Claude + Gemini)
✅ Complex pipelines (prompt → model → parser → database)
✅ Memory/chat history management
✅ RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
✅ Tool-calling agents

content.title: When NOT to Use LangChain
content.body:
Don't use LangChain for:

❌ Simple one-off API calls (just use openai directly)
❌ Quick prototypes where you only need one model
❌ Projects where you want zero dependencies

LangChain adds structure — but structure has a cost. For simple scripts, raw API calls are faster to write.

content.title: The LangChain Package Ecosystem
content.explanation: LangChain isn't one giant library — it's a family of focused packages. Understanding which package does what is the first step to using LangChain effectively.

content.title: langchain-core
content.body:
The foundation. Contains the base abstractions that everything else builds on:

- Runnables (the composable interface)
- Message types (`HumanMessage`, `AIMessage`, `SystemMessage`)
- PromptTemplates
- OutputParsers

You'll import from this package the most.

content.title: langchain-openai
content.body:
The OpenAI integration package. Provides:

- `ChatOpenAI` — wrapper for GPT-4, GPT-3.5
- OpenAIEmbeddings — for creating text embeddings

Install: pip install `langchain-openai`

content.title: langchain-anthropic
content.body:
The Anthropic integration package. Provides:

- `ChatAnthropic` — wrapper for Claude models

Install: pip install `langchain-anthropic`

Notice the pattern? Each provider gets its own package.

content.title: langchain-google-genai
content.body:
The Google integration package. Provides:

- `ChatGoogleGenerativeAI` — wrapper for Gemini models

Install: pip install `langchain-google-genai`

content.title: langchain-community
content.body:
A huge collection of 700+ third-party integrations:

- Vector stores (Pinecone, Weaviate, Chroma)
- Document loaders (PDF, CSV, web pages)
- Tools (Wikipedia, Tavily search)

Install: pip install `langchain-community`

content.title: langchain
content.body:
The main orchestration package. Contains:

- Higher-level chain abstractions
- Agent frameworks
- Memory implementations

Install: pip install langchain

content.title: langgraph
content.body:
The agent orchestration framework (we'll cover this in Lesson 8). Lets you build agents as state machines with:

- Nodes (actions)
- Edges (transitions)
- Loops and conditionals

Install: pip install `langgraph`

content.title: LangChain Architecture Overview
content.description: LangChain's packages work together like layers of a building. langchain-core is the foundation, provider packages are the walls, and langchain/langgraph are the roof.

questions.question: What is the PRIMARY problem that LangChain solves?
options: It makes LLMs faster at generating text
It provides a unified interface to work with multiple LLM providers
It trains custom LLMs from scratch
It replaces the need for prompt engineering
questions.explanation: LangChain's main value is provider abstraction — you write your code once and can swap between GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, or any other model by changing a single import.

stages.hint: Each LLM provider has its own package named langchain-{provider}
stages.explanation: LangChain uses separate packages for each provider. For OpenAI, you install langchain-openai. For Anthropic, it would be langchain-anthropic.

challenge.question: To use OpenAI models with LangChain, you need to install the provider package. Complete the pip install command:

content.title: ChatModels: Your Universal LLM Interface
content.explanation: A ChatModel is LangChain's abstraction for any LLM that works with chat messages. Whether it's GPT-4, Claude, or Gemini — they all share the same interface. Learn once, use everywhere.

content.title: What is a ChatModel?
content.body: A ChatModel is a class that wraps an LLM provider's API. It takes in a list of messages (like a conversation) and returns a response. The key insight: ALL ChatModels have the same `.invoke()` method.

content.title: Creating a ChatModel
content.body:
Here's how simple it is:

```python
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

model = ChatOpenAI(model='gpt-4o-mini')
```

That's it. One import, one line. Now `model` can talk to GPT-4.

content.title: Switching Providers
content.body:
Want to use Claude instead? Change TWO things:

```python
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic

model = ChatAnthropic(model='claude-sonnet-4-20250514')
```

Your entire app code stays the same because both use `.invoke()`.

content.title: The invoke() Method
content.body:
Every ChatModel has an `.invoke()` method. You pass in messages, it returns a response:

```python
response = model.invoke('Hello!')
print(response.content)  # 'Hi there! How can I help?'
```

You can also pass a list of Message objects for more control.

content.title: Configuration Options
content.body:
You can configure any `ChatModel` with:

- `temperature` — creativity (0 = focused, 1 = creative)
- `max_tokens` — maximum response length
- `model` — which specific model to use

```python
model = ChatOpenAI(
    model='gpt-4o-mini',
    temperature=0.7,
    max_tokens=500
)
```

content.title: Async and Streaming
content.body:
ChatModels also support:

- `.ainvoke()` — async version (for web servers)
- `.stream()` — get tokens one at a time (for real-time UI)
- `.batch()` — send multiple prompts at once

These work the same across ALL providers.

content.title: Key Takeaway
content.body: ChatModels are the 'universal remote' of LangChain. Learn `.invoke()`, `.stream()`, and `.batch()` once — and you can talk to any LLM in the world. The API differences between providers are handled for you.

content.title: The Message System: Speaking the LLM's Language
content.explanation: LLMs don't just receive plain text — they receive structured messages with roles. Understanding the message system is crucial for building effective AI applications.

content.title: Why Messages?
content.body: When you chat with ChatGPT, each message has a role: you're the 'user', ChatGPT is the 'assistant', and there's a hidden 'system' message defining its personality. LangChain models this with Message classes.

content.title: HumanMessage
content.body:
Represents what the USER says:


```python
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage
```


```python
msg = HumanMessage(content='What is Python?')
```

This is the most common message type — it's your input to the LLM.

content.title: AIMessage
content.body:
Represents the LLM's response:


```python
from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage
```


```python
msg = AIMessage(content='Python is a programming language.')
```

You typically don't create these manually — the model returns them. But they're useful for building conversation history.

content.title: SystemMessage
content.body:
Sets the LLM's behavior/personality:


```python
from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage
```


```python
msg = SystemMessage(content='You are a helpful coding tutor.')
```

This goes at the start of the conversation and shapes how the LLM responds to everything after.

content.title: Sending a Full Conversation
content.body:
You can send a complete conversation to the model:


```python
response = model.invoke([
```
    SystemMessage(content='You are a Python tutor.'),
    HumanMessage(content='What is a list?'),
    AIMessage(content='A list is a collection of items.'),
    HumanMessage(content='Show me an example.')

```python
])
```

The model sees the full conversation history and responds to the last message.

content.title: Shortcut: Using Tuples
content.body:
LangChain also accepts simple tuples instead of Message objects:


```python
response = model.invoke([
    ('system', 'You are a Python tutor.'),
    ('human', 'What is a list?')
])
```

Same result, less typing. Use whichever style you prefer.

content.title: The response Object
content.body:
When the model responds, you get an `AIMessage` object:


```python
response = model.invoke('Hello!')
print(response.content)    # The text response
print(response.response_metadata)  # Token usage, model info
```

The `.content` property is what you'll use 99% of the time.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a SystemMessage in LangChain?
options: To send error logs to the system console
To define the LLM's behavior, personality, or role for the conversation
To restart the model's memory between conversations
To authenticate the API key with the provider
questions.explanation: A SystemMessage is placed at the start of a conversation to set the LLM's behavior — for example, 'You are a helpful Python tutor' or 'Always respond in JSON format'. It shapes how the model responds to all subsequent messages.

content.title: PromptTemplates: Reusable Prompt Design
content.explanation: Hardcoding prompts is like hardcoding passwords — it works but it's a terrible practice. PromptTemplates let you create reusable, parameterized prompts that you can fill with different values each time.

content.title: The Problem with Hardcoded Prompts
content.body:
Without templates, you end up writing:


```python
prompt = f'You are a {role}. Explain {topic} to a {level} student.'
```

This works for simple cases, but f-strings don't validate variables, can't be serialized, and can't be composed into chains.

content.title: What is a PromptTemplate?
content.body:
A `PromptTemplate` is a reusable prompt blueprint with named placeholders:


```python
from langchain_core.prompts import PromptTemplate
```


```python
template = PromptTemplate.from_template(
```

```python
    'Explain {topic} in simple terms'
```

```python
)
```


```python
result = template.invoke({'topic': 'neural networks'})
# → 'Explain neural networks in simple terms'
```

content.title: ChatPromptTemplate (The One You'll Use Most)
content.body:
For chat models, use `ChatPromptTemplate` — it creates proper message objects:


```python
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
```


```python
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ('system', 'You are a {role}.'),
    ('human', '{question}')
])
```


```python
result = prompt.invoke({'role': 'tutor', 'question': 'What is Python?'})
```

content.title: Why Not Just Use f-strings?
content.body:
PromptTemplates give you superpowers f-strings don't have:

1. Composability — plug into LCEL chains with the | operator
2. Validation — know which variables are required
3. Serialization — save/load prompts from files
4. Partial filling — fill some variables now, others later
5. Type safety — integrates with LangChain's type system

content.title: Variable Placeholders
content.body:
Variables use single curly braces: {variable_name}


```python
template = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ('system', 'You are a {role} who speaks {language}.'),
    ('human', 'Explain {concept}')
])
```


```python
# Required variables: role, language, concept
```

```python
print(template.input_variables)
# → ['role', 'language', 'concept']
```

content.title: Partial Templates
content.body:
Fill some variables now, the rest later:


```python
partial = template.partial(role='Python tutor', language='English')
```


```python
# Now you only need to provide 'concept'
```

```python
result = partial.invoke({'concept': 'decorators'})
```

This is useful when some values are fixed (like role) but others change per request.

content.title: Key Takeaway
content.body: Always use `ChatPromptTemplate` for chat models. It creates proper message objects, validates your variables, and plugs directly into LCEL chains. Think of templates as the 'input layer' of your LangChain pipeline.

questions.question: Why should you use ChatPromptTemplate instead of Python f-strings for prompts?
options: f-strings are slower to execute than templates
ChatPromptTemplate can compose into LCEL chains, validates variables, and creates proper Message objects
ChatPromptTemplate automatically optimizes prompts for better LLM responses

content.title: Output Parsers: Getting Clean Data from LLMs
content.explanation: LLMs return raw text. But your app needs structured data — JSON, lists, typed objects. Output Parsers bridge this gap by transforming messy LLM text into clean, validated data structures.

content.title: The Problem
content.body:
You ask an LLM: 'List 3 Python frameworks'. It might return:

'Sure! Here are 3 frameworks:\n1. Django\n2. Flask\n3. FastAPI'

But your app needs ['Django', 'Flask', 'FastAPI']. How do you reliably convert the LLM's conversational text into clean data?

content.title: StrOutputParser (The Simplest)
content.body:
Extracts just the text content from the LLM's response:


```python
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
```


```python
parser = StrOutputParser()
```


```python
# Use in a chain: prompt | model | parser
```

```python
# Input: AIMessage(content='Hello!')
# Output: 'Hello!' (plain string)
```

This is the most common parser — just give me the text.

content.title: JsonOutputParser
content.body:
Parses the LLM's output as JSON:


```python
from langchain_core.output_parsers import JsonOutputParser
```


```python
parser = JsonOutputParser()
```


```python
# The LLM must return valid JSON
```

```python
# Input: AIMessage(content='{"name": "Django", "type": "web"}')
# Output: {'name': 'Django', 'type': 'web'} (Python dict)
```

content.title: PydanticOutputParser (Type-Safe)
content.body:
The most powerful parser — validates output against a Pydantic model:


```python
from pydantic import BaseModel
from langchain_core.output_parsers import PydanticOutputParser
```


```python
class Movie(BaseModel):
```
    title: str
    year: int
    genre: str


```python
parser = PydanticOutputParser(pydantic_object=Movie)
```

This ensures the LLM returns data matching your exact schema.

content.title: Format Instructions (The Secret Sauce)
content.body:
Parsers can generate instructions that tell the LLM HOW to format its response:


```python
parser = PydanticOutputParser(pydantic_object=Movie)
print(parser.get_format_instructions())
```

# → 'Return a JSON object with fields: title (string), year (integer), genre (string)'

You include these instructions in your prompt so the LLM knows the exact format you expect.

content.title: CommaSeparatedListOutputParser
content.body:
For when you just want a simple list:


```python
from langchain_core.output_parsers import CommaSeparatedListOutputParser
```


```python
parser = CommaSeparatedListOutputParser()
```


```python
# Input: 'Django, Flask, FastAPI'
```

```python
# Output: ['Django', 'Flask', 'FastAPI']
```

content.title: Which Parser to Use?
content.body:
Quick decision guide:

- Just need text? → `StrOutputParser`
- Need a Python dict? → `JsonOutputParser`
- Need validated, typed data? → `PydanticOutputParser`
- Need a simple list? → `CommaSeparatedListOutputParser`

90% of the time, you'll use `StrOutputParser` or `JsonOutputParser`.

content.title: LCEL: The Pipe Operator for AI
content.explanation: LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) is the syntax for connecting components together. If you've ever used Unix pipes (cat file | grep error | sort), LCEL works the same way — but for AI components.

content.title: What is LCEL?
content.body:
LCEL (LangChain Expression Language) is a way to connect LangChain components using the pipe operator |.


```python
chain = prompt | model | parser
```

This reads as: 'Take the prompt output, send it to the model, then parse the result.' Simple, readable, powerful.

content.title: How the Pipe Works
content.body:
Each component's output becomes the next component's input:


```python
1. prompt.invoke({'topic': 'Python'}) → ChatPromptValue
2. model.invoke(ChatPromptValue) → AIMessage
3. parser.invoke(AIMessage) → 'Python is a...'
```

The | operator connects them automatically.

content.title: The Simplest Chain
content.body:
```python
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser
```


```python
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template('Explain {topic}')
model = ChatOpenAI(model='gpt-4o-mini')
parser = StrOutputParser()
```


```python
chain = prompt | model | parser
result = chain.invoke({'topic': 'recursion'})
```

content.title: Why Not Just Call Each Step Manually?
content.body:
You could write:


```python
messages = prompt.invoke({'topic': 'recursion'})
response = model.invoke(messages)
text = parser.invoke(response)
```

But LCEL chains give you FREE superpowers:

```python
- .stream() — streaming for all steps
- .batch() — parallel processing
- .ainvoke() — async support
```
- Automatic error handling and retries

content.title: Adding More Steps
content.body:
You can add any number of steps:


```python
chain = prompt | model | parser | some_function
```

Any Python function that takes input and returns output can be part of a chain. Use `RunnableLambda` to wrap regular functions:


```python
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableLambda
```


```python
uppercase = `RunnableLambda`(lambda x: x.upper())
```

```python
chain = prompt | model | parser | uppercase
```

content.title: RunnablePassthrough (Forwarding Data)
content.body:
Sometimes you need to pass the original input alongside the processed output:


```python
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough
```


```python
chain = {
```
    'context': retriever,
    'question': `RunnablePassthrough`()

```python
} | prompt | model | parser
```

This is essential for RAG chains where you need both the retrieved docs AND the original question.

content.title: Key Takeaway
content.body:
LCEL is the glue that holds LangChain together. The pattern is always:


```python
chain = input_processor | model | output_processor
```

Learn this pattern and you can build any LLM pipeline — from simple chatbots to complex multi-step RAG systems.

content.title: The LCEL Pipeline
content.description: Data flows through an LCEL chain like water through pipes. Each component transforms the data and passes it to the next.

steps.name: User Input
steps.description: Raw user data enters the chain.

steps.name: PromptTemplate
steps.description: Variables are injected into the prompt.

steps.name: ChatModel
steps.description: The language model creates the answer.

steps.name: StrOutputParser
steps.description: Converts model response into usable text.

steps.name: Final Output
steps.output: Python is a programming language used for...
steps.description: Clean result returned to application.

codePanel.title: LCEL Code
codePanel.code:
prompt = PromptTemplate(...)
model = ChatOpenAI(...)
parser = StrOutputParser()

chain = prompt | model | parser

result = chain.invoke(
    {"topic":"Python"}
)

    'Context: {context}\n\nQuestion: {question}\n\nAnswer:'
)

# Build the RAG chain

from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

    'Context: {context}\n\nQuestion: {question}\n\nAnswer:'
)

parser = StrOutputParser()

stages.hint: Think of Unix pipes — the same symbol is used to chain commands together.
stages.explanation: The pipe operator | is the core of LCEL. It connects components so data flows from left to right: prompt → model → parser.

content.title: Memory: Making Your Chatbot Remember
content.explanation: Every LLM API call is stateless — the model forgets everything between calls. If a user says 'My name is Alice' and then asks 'What is my name?', the model has no idea. Memory solves this.

content.title: The Stateless Problem
content.body:
LLMs are like a goldfish — every API call starts with a blank slate.

Call 1: User: 'My name is Alice'
LLM: 'Nice to meet you, Alice!'

Call 2: User: 'What is my name?'
LLM: 'I don't know your name.'

The model literally forgot. Memory fixes this.

content.title: The Solution: Chat History
content.body:
The trick is simple: store all previous messages and send them with every new request. The LLM doesn't actually 'remember' — we just resend the conversation each time.

Call 2 becomes:
[`SystemMessage`, `HumanMessage`('My name is Alice'), `AIMessage`('Nice to meet you!'), `HumanMessage`('What is my name?')]

content.title: ChatMessageHistory
content.body:
LangChain provides a simple in-memory store:


```python
from langchain_core.chat_history import InMemoryChatMessageHistory
```


```python
history = InMemoryChatMessageHistory()
history.add_user_message('My name is Alice')
history.add_ai_message('Nice to meet you, Alice!')
```


```python
print(history.messages)  # List of all messages
```

content.title: RunnableWithMessageHistory
content.body:
To automatically add memory to an LCEL chain:


```python
from langchain_core.runnables.history import RunnableWithMessageHistory
```

chain_with_memory = `RunnableWithMessageHistory`(
    chain,
    get_session_history=lambda `session_id`: history,
    input_messages_key='input',
    history_messages_key='history'

```python
)
```

content.title: Session IDs (Multi-User Support)
content.body:
Each user needs their own conversation history. Use `session_id` to separate them:


```python
store = {}
```


```python
def get_history(session_id):
    if session_id not in store:
```
        store[`session_id`] = `InMemoryChatMessageHistory`()

```python
    return store[session_id]
```


```python
# User 'alice' and 'bob' have separate conversations
```

content.title: Window Memory (Limiting Context)
content.body:
Conversations can get long and expensive. Window memory keeps only the last N messages:


```python
# Manual approach: trim history
```

```python
messages = history.messages[-10:]  # Keep last 10
```

This prevents your token costs from growing indefinitely while keeping recent context.

content.title: Key Takeaway
content.body:
Memory in LangChain is NOT magic — it's just 'resend previous messages with each call'. The framework handles the plumbing:

1. `InMemoryChatMessageHistory` stores messages
2. `RunnableWithMessageHistory` injects them into chains
3. Session IDs separate users

For production, replace in-memory with Redis or PostgreSQL.

content.title: Tools: Giving LLMs Superpowers
content.explanation: LLMs can only generate text — they can't search the web, query databases, or do math reliably. Tools are functions that extend what an LLM can do. The LLM decides WHEN to use a tool, and LangChain handles the execution.

content.title: Why Tools?
content.body:
LLMs have limitations:

- Can't access real-time data (training cutoff)
- Can't do precise math (they guess)
- Can't query your database
- Can't send emails or call APIs

Tools let the LLM say: 'I need to search for X' and LangChain actually does the search.

content.title: What is a Tool?
content.body:
A Tool is just a Python function with a name, description, and type hints. The description tells the LLM WHEN to use it:


```python
@tool
def search_web(query: str) -> str:
```
    '''Search the web for current information.'''

```python
    # ... actual search logic
```

```python
    return results
```

content.title: Creating a Tool with @tool
content.body:
The `@tool` decorator is the easiest way to create a tool:


```python
from langchain_core.tools import tool
```

```python
@tool
def multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int:
```
    '''Multiply two numbers together.'''

```python
    return a * b
```


```python
print(multiply.name)  # 'multiply'
print(multiply.description)  # 'Multiply two numbers together.'
```

content.title: How Tool Calling Works
content.body:
The LLM doesn't run tools itself. Here's the flow:

1. You send a question + available tools to the LLM
2. The LLM says: 'I want to call multiply(3, 7)'
3. YOUR code calls multiply(3, 7) → 21
4. You send the result (21) back to the LLM
5. The LLM uses 21 to form its final answer

LangChain automates steps 2-5.

content.title: Binding Tools to a Model
content.body:
Tell the model which tools it can use:


```python
tools = [multiply, search_web]
model_with_tools = model.bind_tools(tools)
```

Now when you invoke this model, it can choose to call any of the bound tools. The model decides based on the user's question.

content.title: Built-in Tools
content.body:
LangChain provides many pre-built tools:

- TavilySearchResults — web search
- WikipediaQueryRun — Wikipedia lookup
- PythonREPL — run Python code
- RequestsGetTool — make HTTP requests

You can also create custom tools for your specific app (database queries, API calls, etc.).

content.title: Tools vs Functions
content.body:
A regular Python function just runs code. A LangChain Tool is a function that:

1. Has a name and description (so the LLM knows WHAT it does)
2. Has typed parameters (so the LLM knows WHAT to pass)
3. Can be bound to a `ChatModel`
4. Participates in the agent loop

Think of tools as 'LLM-callable functions'.

content.title: Retrievers: Fetching Relevant Documents
content.explanation: A Retriever is a special type of component that takes a query and returns relevant documents. It's the 'R' in RAG — without retrievers, your LLM can only use its training data.

content.title: What is a Retriever?
content.body:
A Retriever takes a text query and returns a list of relevant Document objects. Think of it as a smart search engine:


```python
query = 'How do I deploy to AWS?'
docs = retriever.invoke(query)
# → [Document(page_content='To deploy to AWS...'), ...]
```

content.title: VectorStoreRetriever (Most Common)
content.body:
The most common retriever uses a vector database:

1. Your documents are converted to embeddings (numbers)
2. They're stored in a vector database (Chroma, Pinecone, etc.)
3. When a query comes in, it's also converted to an embedding
4. The database finds the most similar documents

content.title: Creating a Retriever from a Vector Store
content.body:
```python
from langchain_community.vectorstores import Chroma
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings
```


```python
vectorstore = Chroma.from_documents(
```
    documents=docs,
    embedding=OpenAIEmbeddings()

```python
)
```


```python
retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(
```

```python
    search_kwargs={'k': 3}  # Return top 3 results
```

```python
)
```

content.title: The Document Object
content.body:
Retrievers return Document objects:


```python
from langchain_core.documents import Document
```


```python
doc = Document(
    page_content='Python is a programming language.',
```
    metadata={'source': 'wiki', 'page': 42}

```python
)
```


```python
page_content = the actual text
```
metadata = extra info (source, page number, etc.)

content.title: Using Retrievers in Chains
content.body:
Retrievers plug directly into LCEL chains:


```python
chain = {
```
    'context': retriever,
    'question': `RunnablePassthrough`()

```python
} | prompt | model | parser
```

The retriever fetches relevant docs, which become the {context} in your prompt. The user's question goes through `RunnablePassthrough`().

content.title: Other Types of Retrievers
content.body:
LangChain supports many retriever types beyond vector stores:

- `BM25Retriever` — keyword-based search
- `MultiQueryRetriever` — generates multiple queries for better recall
- `SelfQueryRetriever` — extracts filters from natural language
- `EnsembleRetriever` — combines multiple retrievers

content.title: Tools vs Retrievers
content.body:
Both fetch external data, but they're different:

- Retriever: Automatic — always runs as part of the chain
- Tool: On-demand — the LLM decides whether to use it

Use retrievers for RAG pipelines (always need context). Use tools for optional actions (search web, run code).

challenge.hint: Use the @tool decorator, add a docstring inside triple quotes, and return a + b.
challenge.explanation: The @tool decorator converts a regular Python function into a LangChain Tool. The docstring becomes the tool's description, which the LLM reads to decide when to use it. Type hints tell the LLM what parameters to pass.

Creates reusable prompts with variable placeholders
Converts raw LLM text into structured data
A function the LLM can decide to call
Fetches relevant documents from external sources

options: Retrievers always run in the chain; Tools are optionally called by the LLM
Tools work with text, Retrievers work with images
Retrievers are for local data, Tools are for cloud data
questions.explanation: Retrievers are automatic — they always run as part of the chain to fetch context. Tools are on-demand — the LLM decides whether to call them based on the user's question.

content.title: LangGraph: From Chains to Agents
content.explanation: Chains are great for linear workflows (A → B → C). But what if you need the LLM to make decisions, loop back, or try different approaches? That's where LangGraph comes in — it lets you build agents as state machines.

content.title: Why Not Just Use Chains?
content.body:
Chains are linear: prompt → model → parser. Done.

But real agents need to:
- Make decisions (if the answer is unclear, search again)
- Loop (keep trying until successful)
- Branch (use different tools for different questions)

Chains can't do this. LangGraph can.

content.title: What is LangGraph?
content.body:
LangGraph models your agent as a directed graph:

- Nodes = Actions (call LLM, use a tool, format output)
- Edges = Transitions (go from node A to node B)
- State = Shared data that flows through the graph

Think of it as a flowchart that your code actually executes.

content.title: The Three Building Blocks
content.body:
Every LangGraph agent has:

1. State — a `TypedDict` defining what data the graph tracks
2. Nodes — Python functions that process the state
3. Edges — connections between nodes (can be conditional)

That's it. Everything else is built from these three primitives.

content.title: State: The Agent's Memory
content.body:
State is a `TypedDict` that holds all data flowing through the graph:


```python
from typing import TypedDict, Annotated
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages
```


```python
class AgentState(TypedDict):
```
    messages: Annotated[list, `add_messages`]
    current_step: str

The 'messages' field uses `add_messages` to automatically append (not overwrite) messages.

content.title: Nodes: The Workers
content.body:
A node is just a function that takes state and returns updates:


```python
def chatbot(state: AgentState):
    response = model.invoke(state['messages'])
    return {'messages': [response]}
```

The function reads from state, does its work, and returns a dict of updates. LangGraph merges the updates into the state.

content.title: Edges: The Connections
content.body:
Edges define the flow between nodes:


```python
# Standard edge: always go from A to B
```

```python
graph.add_edge('node_a', 'node_b')
```


```python
# Conditional edge: choose based on state
```

```python
graph.add_conditional_edges(
```
    'agent',
    should_continue,  # function that returns 'tool' or 'end'

```python
    {'tool': 'tool_node', 'end': END}
```

```python
)
```

content.title: Chains vs LangGraph
content.body:
Use Chains (LCEL) when:
✅ Linear workflow (A → B → C)
✅ No decision-making needed
✅ Simple prompt → model → parser

Use LangGraph when:
✅ Agent needs to make decisions
✅ Loops (retry, iterate)
✅ Multiple tools with routing
✅ Human-in-the-loop approvals
✅ Complex multi-step workflows

content.title: Chain vs LangGraph Architecture
content.description: Chains are linear pipelines. LangGraph agents are graphs with loops, branches, and decisions.

comparisonPanel.title: Key Differences: LCEL Chain vs LangGraph

left.title: LCEL CHAIN
left.description: A Chain follows a predefined sequence of steps. Each component executes exactly once in order.

right.title: LANGGRAPH
right.description: LangGraph enables stateful agents that can reason, make decisions, call tools, loop, and collaborate.

content.title: Building a StateGraph Step by Step
content.explanation: Let's walk through building a complete LangGraph agent from scratch — one step at a time.

content.title: Step 1: Define the State
content.body:
```python
from typing import TypedDict, Annotated
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages
```


```python
class State(TypedDict):
```
    messages: Annotated[list, `add_messages`]

This creates a state with one field: messages. The `add_messages` annotation means new messages are APPENDED (not replaced).

content.title: Step 2: Create the Graph
content.body:
```python
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph
```


```python
graph_builder = StateGraph(State)
```
StateGraph takes your State class as input. It creates a builder object that you'll add nodes and edges to.

content.title: Step 3: Add Nodes
content.body:
```python
def chatbot(state: State):
    response = model.invoke(state['messages'])
    return {'messages': [response]}
```

```python
graph_builder.add_node('chatbot', chatbot)
```

Each node has a name (string) and a function. The function takes state and returns a dict of updates.

content.title: Step 4: Set Entry Point
content.body:
```python
graph_builder.set_entry_point('chatbot')
```

This tells LangGraph which node to execute FIRST when the graph is invoked. Every graph needs exactly one entry point.

content.title: Step 5: Set Finish Point
content.body:
```python
graph_builder.set_finish_point('chatbot')
```


```python
# Or use the END constant:
```

```python
from langgraph.graph import END
graph_builder.add_edge('chatbot', END)
```

This tells LangGraph when to STOP executing and return the final state.

content.title: Step 6: Compile the Graph
content.body:
```python
graph = graph_builder.compile()
```

Compilation validates your graph (checks for missing edges, unreachable nodes) and returns an executable graph object. You MUST compile before invoking.

content.title: Step 7: Run It!
content.body:
```python
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage
```


```python
result = graph.invoke({
```
    'messages': [`HumanMessage`(content='Hello!')]

```python
})
```


```python
print(result['messages'][-1].content)
# → 'Hi there! How can I help you?'
```

challenge.title: Building a Simple StateGraph
challenge.question: Create a basic LangGraph StateGraph. Define a State with a 'messages' field (using Annotated with add_messages). Create a StateGraph, add a 'chatbot' node, set it as both entry and finish point, and compile the graph. Store the compiled graph in a variable called 'graph'.
challenge.starterCode:

    messages: Annotated[list, add_messages]

# Step 2: Define node function
def chatbot(state: State):

# Step 3: Build and compile the graph
graph_builder = StateGraph(State)
graph_builder.add_node('chatbot', chatbot)
# Set entry and finish points, then compile
___
challenge.solution:
from typing import TypedDict, Annotated
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages

class State(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list, add_messages]

def chatbot(state: State):
    return {'messages': ['Hello from the chatbot!']}

graph_builder = StateGraph(State)
graph_builder.add_node('chatbot', chatbot)
graph_builder.set_entry_point('chatbot')
graph_builder.set_finish_point('chatbot')
graph = graph_builder.compile()
challenge.hint: Use graph_builder.set_entry_point('chatbot'), graph_builder.set_finish_point('chatbot'), then graph = graph_builder.compile().
challenge.explanation: This is the minimal LangGraph agent. The StateGraph holds the state definition. We add a node, set where execution starts and ends, then compile it into an executable graph.

challenge.title: Adding Conditional Edges
challenge.question: Create a routing function called 'should_continue' that checks the last message in state['messages']. If the last message contains 'DONE', return 'end'. Otherwise, return 'continue'. This function will be used for conditional routing in a LangGraph agent.
challenge.starterCode:
from langgraph.graph import END

def should_continue(state):
    # Get the last message
    last_message = state['messages'][-1]
    # Check if it contains 'DONE'
    # Return 'end' if done, 'continue' if not
    pass
challenge.hint: Check if 'DONE' is in the string representation of the last message. Return 'end' or 'continue'.
challenge.explanation: Conditional edge functions inspect the current state and return a string that maps to the next node. LangGraph uses this to decide which path to take — enabling loops, branching, and dynamic routing.

content.title: The Easy Way: create_react_agent
content.explanation: Building a StateGraph from scratch gives you full control. But for common patterns, LangGraph provides pre-built agents that handle all the boilerplate for you.

content.title: What is create_react_agent?
content.body:
`create_react_agent` builds a complete tool-calling agent in ONE function call:


```python
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
```


```python
agent = create_react_agent(model, tools)
```

That's it. No `StateGraph`, no nodes, no edges. It handles everything.

content.title: How It Works
content.body:
`create_react_agent` creates a graph with:

1. An 'agent' node (calls the LLM)
2. A 'tools' node (executes tool calls)
3. A conditional edge (loop between agent and tools until done)

The ReAct pattern: Reason → Act → Observe → Repeat

content.title: Full Example
content.body:
```python
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_core.tools import tool
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent
```

```python
@tool
def search(query: str) -> str:
```
    '''Search the web for information.'''

```python
    return f'Results for: {query}'
```


```python
model = ChatOpenAI(model='gpt-4o-mini')
agent = create_react_agent(model, [search])
```


```python
result = agent.invoke({
```
    'messages': [('human', 'Search for Python tutorials')]

```python
})
```

content.title: Adding a System Prompt
content.body:
Customize the agent's behavior:


```python
agent = create_react_agent(
```
    model,
    tools,

```python
    prompt='You are a helpful research assistant. Always cite your sources.'
)
```

The system prompt shapes how the agent reasons about which tools to use.

content.title: When to Use create_react_agent
content.body:
Use it when you want a standard tool-calling agent:

✅ LLM + Tools pattern
✅ Simple reasoning loops
✅ Quick prototypes

Build a custom `StateGraph` when:
❌ Multi-agent systems
❌ Complex routing logic
❌ Human-in-the-loop approvals
❌ Custom state beyond messages

content.title: Streaming with the Agent
content.body:
The agent supports streaming out of the box:


```python
for event in agent.stream({'messages': [('human', 'Search for AI news')]}):
    for node_name, output in event.items():
        print(f'{node_name}: {output}')
```

You see each step as it happens: the LLM thinking, the tool executing, the final response.

content.title: Key Takeaway
content.body: Start with `create_react_agent` for 90% of use cases. It handles the ReAct loop, tool execution, and error handling. Only build a custom `StateGraph` when you need full control over the agent's decision flow.

content.title: State Design: The Heart of Every LangGraph Agent
content.explanation: The State is the single most important design decision in LangGraph. It defines WHAT your agent knows and HOW data flows through every node. Get State right, and everything else falls into place.

content.title: State is a TypedDict
content.body:
Every LangGraph agent starts with a State definition using Python's `TypedDict`:


```python
from typing import TypedDict
```


```python
class AgentState(TypedDict):
```
    messages: list
    user_query: str
    search_results: list

This defines the 'shape' of data flowing through your graph — like a database schema for your agent.

content.title: Why TypedDict?
content.body:
`TypedDict` gives you:

- Type checking — catch bugs before runtime
- Auto-completion — your IDE knows the fields
- Documentation — anyone reading your code knows what the state contains
- Validation — LangGraph checks that nodes return valid state updates

Plain dicts work but `TypedDict` is the professional approach.

content.title: The Problem: Overwriting vs Appending
content.body:
When a node returns {'messages': [new_msg]}, should it:

A) REPLACE the entire messages list? (overwrite)
B) ADD new_msg to the existing list? (append)

By default, LangGraph OVERWRITES. But for chat history, you want APPEND. This is where Reducers come in.

content.title: Reducers: Controlling How State Updates
content.body:
A Reducer is a function that decides HOW to merge a node's output into the state:


```python
from typing import Annotated
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages
```


```python
class AgentState(TypedDict):
```
    messages: Annotated[list, `add_messages`]  # APPEND
    user_query: str                          # OVERWRITE (default)

`add_messages` is a built-in reducer that appends new messages to the list instead of replacing it.

content.title: The add_messages Reducer
content.body:
`add_messages` is the most important reducer. It:

1. Appends new messages to the existing list
2. Handles deduplication (won't add the same message twice)
3. Supports message deletion via `RemoveMessage`


```python
class State(TypedDict):
```
    messages: Annotated[list, `add_messages`]


```python
# Node returns {'messages': [`AIMessage`('Hi')]}
```

```python
# Result: existing messages + AIMessage('Hi')
```

content.title: Custom Reducers
content.body:
You can write your own reducer — it's just a function that takes (old_value, new_value) and returns the merged result:


```python
def add_to_set(existing: set, new_items: set) -> set:
    return existing | new_items  # Union
```


```python
class State(TypedDict):
```
    visited_urls: Annotated[set, add_to_set]

Now visited_urls accumulates URLs instead of replacing them.

content.title: State Design Best Practices
content.body:
1. Always use Annotated + `add_messages` for message fields
2. Keep state flat — avoid deeply nested dicts
3. Only include data that multiple nodes need to share
4. Use descriptive field names (not 'data' or 'stuff')
5. Add type hints to every field
6. Consider what each node reads vs. writes

content.title: Edges & Routing: Controlling Agent Flow
content.explanation: Edges are what make LangGraph powerful. Standard edges create fixed paths. Conditional edges let your agent make decisions at runtime. Together, they let you build agents that think, act, and adapt.

content.title: Three Types of Edges
content.body:
LangGraph supports three edge types:

1. Standard Edge — always go from A to B
2. Conditional Edge — choose next node based on state
3. Entry Edge — where execution starts


```python
graph.add_edge('a', 'b')          # Standard
graph.add_conditional_edges(...)   # Conditional
graph.set_entry_point('start')     # Entry
```

content.title: Standard Edges
content.body:
The simplest connection — unconditional, always followed:


```python
graph.add_edge('fetch_data', 'process_data')
graph.add_edge('process_data', 'generate_report')
```

This creates: fetch_data → process_data → generate_report. Like a chain, but inside a graph.

content.title: Conditional Edges (The Power Feature)
content.body:
Conditional edges let the agent choose its path:


```python
def route_decision(state):
    if state['needs_search']:
        return 'search_node'
    return 'answer_node'
```

```python
graph.add_conditional_edges(
```
    'agent',           # From this node
    route_decision,    # This function decides
    {                  # Map return values to nodes
        'search_node': 'search',
        'answer_node': 'answer'

```python
    }
)
```

content.title: The Routing Function
content.body:
The routing function:
1. Takes the current state as input
2. Inspects the state to make a decision
3. Returns a STRING that maps to the next node


```python
def router(state):
```

```python
    last_msg = state['messages'][-1]
```

```python
    if last_msg.tool_calls:  # LLM wants to use a tool
        return 'tools'
    return 'end'             # LLM has the final answer
```

This is how tool-calling agents decide whether to loop.

content.title: The END Constant
content.body:
Use END to terminate the graph:


```python
from langgraph.graph import END
```

```python
graph.add_conditional_edges(
```
    'agent',
    router,

```python
    {'tools': 'tool_node', 'end': END}
```

```python
)
```

When the router returns 'end', the graph stops executing and returns the final state.

content.title: Creating Loops (The Agent Loop)
content.body:
The real magic — making agents that LOOP:


```python
# Agent calls LLM
```

```python
# If LLM wants a tool → go to tool_node
# Tool_node executes → go BACK to agent
# Agent calls LLM again with tool results
# If LLM has answer → END
```

```python
graph.add_edge('tool_node', 'agent')  # Loop back!
graph.add_conditional_edges('agent', router, ...)
```

This loop continues until the LLM decides it's done.

content.title: Multiple Branches (Fan-Out)
content.body:
Send state to MULTIPLE nodes simultaneously:


```python
def parallel_router(state):
    return ['search', 'database']  # Both run!
```

Or use a list in add_edge:

```python
graph.add_edge('start', ['search', 'database'])
```

Both search and database nodes run in parallel, and their results are merged back into state.

content.title: Checkpointers: Persistent Agent Memory
content.explanation: By default, a LangGraph agent forgets everything after each invocation. Checkpointers save the graph's state after every step — enabling conversation memory, session persistence, and even time travel (undoing steps).

content.title: The Problem Without Checkpointers
content.body:
```python
Without checkpointers, every graph.invoke() call starts fresh:
```


```python
result1 = graph.invoke({'messages': [('human', 'My name is Alice')]})
# Agent: 'Nice to meet you, Alice!'
```


```python
result2 = graph.invoke({'messages': [('human', 'What is my name?')]})
# Agent: 'I don't know your name.'
```

The agent forgot Alice. Checkpointers fix this.

content.title: What is a Checkpointer?
content.body:
A Checkpointer saves the state after EVERY node execution. Think of it as auto-save in a video game:

- After node 1 runs → save state
- After node 2 runs → save state
- After node 3 runs → save state

You can resume from any checkpoint, replay steps, or even go back in time.

content.title: MemorySaver (In-Memory Checkpointer)
content.body:
The simplest checkpointer — stores state in RAM:


```python
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
```


```python
checkpointer = MemorySaver()
graph = graph_builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)
```

Perfect for development and testing. Data is lost when the process restarts.

content.title: Thread IDs: Separating Conversations
content.body:
Each conversation needs a unique `thread_id`:


```python
config = {'configurable': {'thread_id': 'conversation_001'}}
```


```python
result = graph.invoke(
    {'messages': [('human', 'My name is Alice')]},
    config=config
)
```


```python
# Same `thread_id` = same conversation
```

```python
result2 = graph.invoke(
    {'messages': [('human', 'What is my name?')]},
    config=config  # SAME thread_id!
)
```

```python
# Agent: 'Your name is Alice!'
```

content.title: How It Works Under the Hood
content.body:
When you invoke with a `thread_id`:

1. LangGraph checks if a checkpoint exists for that thread
2. If yes → loads the previous state (including all messages)
3. Runs the graph with the loaded state + your new input
4. Saves the new state back to the checkpointer

The agent 'remembers' because it reloads all previous messages.

content.title: Production Checkpointers
content.body:
For production, use persistent storage:

- `PostgresSaver` — PostgreSQL database
- `SqliteSaver` — SQLite file
- `RedisSaver` — Redis cache


```python
from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres import PostgresSaver
```


```python
checkpointer = PostgresSaver(conn_string='postgresql://...')
graph = graph_builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)
```

Now conversations survive server restarts.

content.title: Key Takeaway
content.body:
Checkpointers = agent memory that persists across invocations.

1. Use `MemorySaver` for development
2. Use `PostgresSaver` for production
3. Always pass `thread_id` in config
4. Same `thread_id` = same conversation
5. Different `thread_id` = fresh conversation

This is how you build chatbots that remember users.

content.title: Streaming: Real-Time Agent Execution
content.explanation: Users hate waiting. Streaming shows the agent's progress in real-time — each node's output appears as it completes, creating a responsive, interactive experience.

content.title: Why Stream?
content.body:
Without streaming, users see nothing until the entire graph finishes:


```python
❌ graph.invoke() → [blank screen for 10 seconds] → full answer
```

With streaming, users see each step as it happens:


```python
✅ graph.stream() → Agent thinking... → Searching... → Found 3 results... → Here's your answer
```

content.title: The .stream() Method
Stream Modes
content.body:
LangGraph supports different streaming granularities:

- 'values' — full state after each node (default)
- 'updates' — only what changed at each node
- 'messages' — individual LLM tokens as they generate


```python
for event in graph.stream(input, stream_mode='updates'):
    print(event)  # Only the delta
```

content.title: Token-Level Streaming
content.body:
Stream individual tokens as the LLM generates them:


```python
for event in graph.stream(input, stream_mode='messages'):
    # event is (message_chunk, metadata)
```
    msg, meta = event

```python
    print(msg.content, end='', flush=True)
```

This gives the classic ChatGPT typing effect — text appears character by character.

content.title: Async Streaming (For Web Servers)
content.body:
For FastAPI/Django, use async streaming:


```python
async for event in graph.astream(input):
    for node, output in event.items():
        yield f'data: {json.dumps(output)}\n\n'
```

This integrates with Server-Sent Events (SSE) for real-time web UI updates.

content.title: Streaming with Checkpointers
Key Takeaway
content.body:
```python
Always use .stream() in production:
```

- Better UX — users see progress immediately
- Lower perceived latency — feels faster
- Debuggability — see each node's output
- Resilience — checkpoints at each step


```python
Use .invoke() only for testing and batch processing.
```

content.title: Human-in-the-Loop: Agent Safety Gates
content.explanation: Some actions are too risky for an agent to take alone — sending emails, making purchases, deleting data. Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) lets you pause the agent and ask for human approval before continuing.

content.title: Why Human-in-the-Loop?
content.body:
Imagine an AI agent that can:
- Send emails on your behalf
- Execute database queries
- Make API calls that cost money

You probably want to review these actions BEFORE the agent executes them. HITL adds approval gates.

content.title: interrupt_before: Pause Before a Node
content.body:
Pause execution BEFORE a specific node runs:


```python
graph = graph_builder.compile(
    checkpointer=checkpointer,
```
    `interrupt_before`=['send_email']  # Pause here!

```python
)
```

When the graph reaches 'send_email', it STOPS and returns the current state. You review it, then resume.

content.title: interrupt_after: Pause After a Node
content.body:
Pause execution AFTER a node runs (to review its output):


```python
graph = graph_builder.compile(
    checkpointer=checkpointer,
```
    `interrupt_after`=['tool_node']  # Pause after tools run

```python
)
```

This lets you see what the tool returned before the agent continues reasoning.

content.title: Resuming Execution
content.body:
After reviewing, resume with None:


```python
# Agent pauses at interrupt
```

```python
for event in graph.stream(input, config):
    print(event)  # Shows state up to the interrupt
```


```python
# Human reviews and approves
```

```python
# Resume by invoking with None
for event in graph.stream(None, config):
    print(event)  # Continues from where it paused
```

content.title: Modifying State Before Resuming
content.body:
You can even CHANGE the state before resuming:


```python
graph.update_state(
```
    config,

```python
    {'messages': [('human', 'Actually, change the subject line')]}
)
```


```python
# Then resume
```

```python
for event in graph.stream(None, config):
    print(event)
```

This lets humans correct the agent's plan before execution.

content.title: HITL Requires a Checkpointer
content.body:
Human-in-the-loop ONLY works with a checkpointer:


```python
graph = graph_builder.compile(
    checkpointer=MemorySaver(),      # Required!
```
    `interrupt_before`=['dangerous_node']

```python
)
```

The checkpointer saves the paused state so you can resume later — even minutes or hours later.

content.title: Common HITL Patterns
content.body:
Typical interrupt points:

- Before tool execution — review which tool and arguments
- Before sending data — review emails, messages, API calls
- After research — review findings before generating report
- Before payment — approve purchases or subscriptions

HITL makes agents safe for production use.

content.title: Multi-Agent Patterns: Teams of Specialized Agents
content.explanation: One agent doing everything is like one person running an entire company. Multi-agent patterns let you create teams of specialized agents — a researcher, a writer, a reviewer — that collaborate to solve complex problems.

content.title: Why Multiple Agents?
content.body:
A single agent with 20 tools gets confused — it doesn't know which tool to use. But split the work:

- Research Agent — has search tools
- Writer Agent — has writing tools
- Reviewer Agent — has evaluation tools

Each agent is focused and effective.

content.title: Subgraphs: Graphs Inside Graphs
content.body:
A Subgraph is a complete LangGraph agent used as a node inside a larger graph:


```python
# Build a sub-agent
```
research_graph = build_research_agent()


```python
# Use it as a node in the main graph
```

```python
main_graph.add_node('research', research_graph)
```

The main graph sends state to the subgraph, which runs its own internal flow and returns results.

content.title: The Supervisor Pattern
content.body:
A 'Supervisor' agent that routes tasks to specialized workers:

1. User sends a query
2. Supervisor decides: 'This needs research'
3. Routes to Research Agent
4. Research Agent returns results
5. Supervisor decides: 'Now write a report'
6. Routes to Writer Agent
7. Writer Agent returns report
8. Supervisor: 'Done!' → END

content.title: Building a Supervisor
content.body:
```python
def supervisor_node(state):
    # LLM decides which worker to route to
    decision = llm.invoke(
```

```python
        f'Given this task: {state["task"]}, '
```
        f'choose: research, writer, or done'

```python
    )
    return {'next_worker': decision.content}
```


```python
# Conditional edges from supervisor
```

```python
graph.add_conditional_edges(
```
    'supervisor',
    lambda state: state['next_worker'],
    {'research': 'research_agent', 'writer': 'writer_agent', 'done': END}

```python
)
```

content.title: Shared State Between Agents
content.body:
All agents in a multi-agent system share the same State:


```python
class TeamState(TypedDict):
```
    messages: Annotated[list, `add_messages`]
    task: str
    research_results: list
    draft: str
    next_worker: str

Each agent reads what it needs and writes its output. The state is the shared workspace.

content.title: The Map-Reduce Pattern
content.body:
Process multiple items in parallel, then combine results:

1. Split: Break a task into subtasks
2. Map: Send each subtask to an agent (in parallel)
3. Reduce: Combine all results into a final output

Example: Analyze 10 documents → 10 agents summarize in parallel → 1 agent combines summaries

content.title: Choosing a Pattern
content.body:
Quick decision guide:

- Simple tool-calling → `create_react_agent` (no multi-agent)
- Complex routing → Supervisor pattern
- Independent subtasks → Map-Reduce pattern
- Nested complexity → Subgraphs
- Team collaboration → Supervisor + Workers

Start simple. Only add multi-agent when a single agent struggles.

content.title: What Are AI Agents?
content.explanation: AI Agents represent the frontier of applied Generative AI. Unlike passive chatbots that simply respond to prompts, agents are autonomous systems that perceive their environment, reason about goals, take actions using tools, and learn from the outcomes — all without constant human intervention.

content.title: Beginner Explanation
content.body: Imagine hiring a brilliant intern. You don't dictate every keystroke — you say 'Research our top 5 competitors and build a comparison spreadsheet.' The intern browses websites, reads reports, compiles data, and delivers the finished work. An AI Agent works identically: you give it a goal, and it autonomously figures out the steps to achieve it.

content.title: How Agents Differ from Chatbots
content.body: A chatbot (like vanilla ChatGPT) is reactive — it answers one question, then waits. An Agent is proactive — it runs in the background for minutes or hours, calling APIs, reading files, writing code, and checking its own work until the goal is fully complete.

content.title: Internal Working
content.body:
Under the hood, an agent wraps an LLM inside an orchestration loop. The loop follows a cycle:

1. Observe the current state

2. Think about what to do next

3. Act by calling a tool

4. Observe the tool's output

5. Decide if the goal is met or if more steps are needed. This loop continues until completion or a safety limit is hit.

content.title: The Agent = LLM + Tools + Memory + Loop
content.body: The LLM is the brain (reasoning engine). Tools are the hands and senses (APIs, web browsers, code interpreters). Memory is the notebook (conversation history, vector databases). The orchestration loop is the nervous system that connects everything.

content.title: Why Agents Matter Now
content.body:
Three breakthroughs converged:

1. LLMs became reliable enough at structured output (JSON) to trigger real APIs

2. Function Calling was built natively into models like GPT-4 and Gemini, and

3. Frameworks like LangGraph and CrewAI made orchestration accessible to any developer.

content.title: Real-World Applications
content.body: Coding agents (Devin, Cursor) that read GitHub issues and submit PRs. Customer support agents that actually process refunds via Stripe. Research agents that spend hours browsing the web and writing 50-page reports. Sales agents that research prospects and draft personalized outreach.

content.title: Enterprise Perspective
content.body: Enterprises are shifting from 'Chat with our Docs' (RAG chatbots) to 'Automate our Workflows' (Agentic systems). The challenge is no longer 'can the AI write an email?' but 'can the AI securely access our CRM, understand the customer's history, resolve their ticket, and comply with GDPR — all autonomously?'

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

# A minimal "agent loop" — the core pattern behind all AI agents
def simple_agent(user_query):
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant. Think step by step."},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_query}
    ]
    
    while True:
        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4o",
            messages=messages
        )
        
        reply = response.choices[0].message.content
        print(f"Agent: {reply}")
        
        # In a real agent, you'd check if a tool call was made
        # and loop back. Here we just return.
        return reply

simple_agent("What is 25 * 4 + 10?")
```

cards.back: A chatbot is reactive (responds to one prompt and waits). An Agent is proactive and autonomous — it runs in the background, calling tools and making decisions until a goal is fully achieved.

content.title: The ReAct Framework
content.explanation: ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) is the foundational paradigm that powers most modern AI agents. It interleaves the model's chain-of-thought reasoning with concrete tool actions, creating a powerful feedback loop between thinking and doing.

content.title: What is ReAct?
content.body: ReAct stands for 'Reasoning + Acting'. It was introduced in a landmark 2022 paper by Yao et al. The core insight: if you force an LLM to write out its reasoning (Thought) before each action (Act), and then observe the result (Observation), it dramatically outperforms both pure reasoning and pure acting approaches.

content.title: The ReAct Loop
content.body: Step 1: THOUGHT — The LLM reasons about what it needs to do next. Step 2: ACTION — The LLM outputs a structured tool call (e.g., search the web for 'Tesla stock price'). Step 3: OBSERVATION — The system executes the tool and returns the result to the LLM. Step 4: REPEAT — The LLM reads the observation, thinks again, and decides if it needs another action or can give a final answer.

content.title: Why Thought Matters
content.body: Without the Thought step, an LLM might impulsively call the wrong tool or pass incorrect arguments. The explicit reasoning step acts as a 'scratchpad' — it forces the model to plan before acting, catching errors before they happen.

content.title: ReAct vs. Chain-of-Thought
content.body: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) only thinks — it cannot act on the world. ReAct combines CoT's reasoning with the ability to call external tools, making it far more capable for real-world tasks that require information retrieval or computation.

content.title: Practical Example
content.body: User: 'What is the market cap of Apple divided by the market cap of Microsoft?' → THOUGHT: I need to look up both market caps. → ACTION: search('Apple market cap 2024') → OBSERVATION: $3.5 trillion → THOUGHT: Now I need Microsoft's. → ACTION: search('Microsoft market cap 2024') → OBSERVATION: $3.1 trillion → THOUGHT: 3.5 / 3.1 = 1.129. → FINAL ANSWER: Apple's market cap is approximately 1.13x Microsoft's.

content.title: Self-Correction
content.body: If a tool returns an error (e.g., 'API rate limit exceeded'), the ReAct pattern naturally handles it: the LLM observes the error, thinks about an alternative (e.g., 'I'll wait 5 seconds and retry' or 'I'll use a different API'), and adapts.

content.title: Implementation
content.body: In frameworks like LangChain and LangGraph, ReAct is implemented as a loop: call the LLM → check if the response contains a tool_call → if yes, execute the tool and feed the result back → if no, return the final answer to the user.

content.example:

Use the following format:

Action Input: the input to the action
Observation: the result of the action
... (this Thought/Action/Action Input/Observation can repeat N times)

content.title: Tool Calling & Function Calling
content.explanation: Tool Calling is the mechanism that gives agents their 'hands'. It allows an LLM to invoke external functions — APIs, databases, code interpreters — by outputting structured JSON instead of plain text. Function Calling is the specific implementation of this by model providers like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic.

content.title: The Core Problem
content.body: LLMs generate text. But text cannot book a flight, send an email, or query a database. To bridge this gap, we need a way for the LLM to express 'I want to call this function with these arguments' in a format that code can parse and execute.

content.title: Tool Definition (The Schema)
content.body: You describe available tools to the LLM using JSON Schema. Each tool has a name, description (so the LLM knows when to use it), and parameter definitions (with types and required fields). Example: {name: 'get_weather', description: 'Get current weather for a city', parameters: {location: string, unit: 'celsius' | 'fahrenheit'}}.

content.title: Native Function Calling
content.body: Modern LLMs (GPT-4, Gemini, Claude) are fine-tuned specifically to output function call JSON when they detect a tool is needed. This is NOT prompt engineering — it is built into the model's training. The model returns a special 'tool_calls' field in the API response instead of regular text.

content.title: The Execution Pipeline
content.body: Step 1: Send user message + tool schemas to LLM. Step 2: LLM decides to call a tool and returns JSON arguments. Step 3: YOUR code (not the LLM) executes the actual function. Step 4: You send the function's result back to the LLM as a 'tool message'. Step 5: LLM generates the final user-facing response incorporating the tool's data.

content.title: Parallel Tool Calls
content.body: Advanced models can request multiple tool calls simultaneously. For example, if the user asks 'What is the weather in London AND New York?', the model can output two parallel tool calls in a single response, dramatically reducing latency.

content.title: Validation with Pydantic
content.body: Never trust the LLM's JSON blindly. Use validation libraries like Pydantic (Python) or Zod (TypeScript) to validate that the LLM's arguments match the expected schema. If validation fails, send the error back to the LLM and ask it to retry — this is the self-correction loop.

content.title: Security Considerations
content.body:
Tool calling is powerful but dangerous. An LLM might hallucinate a destructive API call (e.g., DELETE /users/all). Always implement:

1. Whitelisted tool names

2. Input sanitization

3. Rate limiting

4. Human-in-the-loop approval for destructive operations.

content.title: Defining a Tool Schema
content.explanation: To give an LLM access to a tool, you must define its structure using JSON Schema. This tells the LLM what the tool does and what arguments it requires.

content.title: The Name & Description
content.body: Every tool needs a `name` and a `description`. The description is arguably the most important field—it acts as the instruction manual the LLM reads to decide if and when to trigger the tool. If it is vague, the LLM will hallucinate.

content.title: The Parameters Object
content.body: The `parameters` field must be defined as a JSON Schema `object`. This tells the model that the arguments will be passed as key-value pairs.

content.title: Properties
content.body: Inside `parameters`, the `properties` object defines the specific arguments the tool accepts, including their data types (string, integer, boolean) and descriptions.

content.title: Required Fields
content.body: The `required` array lists which properties must be provided. If you omit an argument here, the LLM might decide not to send it, breaking your backend code.

content.title: Putting It All Together
