# Endpoint 1: Health check at '/health'

# Endpoint 2: Greet by name at '/greet/{name}'
challenge.hint: Use @app.get("/health") for the first endpoint. For the second, use @app.get("/greet/{name}") and make sure the function parameter 'name' matches the path parameter.

content.title: POST Requests & Sending Data (Placing an Order)
content.explanation:
So far, we've only used **GET** requests — which are like LOOKING at the menu. But in AI applications, the most important thing is **sending data TO the server** — like actually PLACING an order.

This is where **POST** requests come in.

**The Problem:**
With GET, you can only send tiny bits of data in the URL (like `/greet/Rahul`). But what if you need to send a whole paragraph to a chatbot? Or a complex form with 10 fields? You can't fit all that in a URL!

**The Solution — POST with a Request Body:**
With POST, you send data inside the 'body' of the request — like putting your order on a piece of paper and handing it to the waiter, instead of yelling it across the restaurant.

**How to Receive POST Data in FastAPI — Pydantic Models:**

FastAPI uses something called a **Pydantic Model** to define what data you expect to receive. Think of it as an order form — it specifies exactly what fields are required.

A Pydantic model is just a Python class that defines:
- What fields should be in the data
- What TYPE each field should be (string, number, etc.)
- Which fields are required and which are optional

If someone sends data that doesn't match the form (like sending a string where a number should be), FastAPI automatically rejects it with a helpful error message. You don't need to write any validation code yourself!
content.tip: Pydantic Models are like order forms — they make sure the data you receive is exactly the right shape and type. FastAPI checks this automatically, so you never have to write 'if message is None: return error' yourself!

content.title: GET vs POST — The Difference
diagram: Data is in the URL (visible to everyone)
Used for: Fetching info, health checks
Data is in the BODY (hidden, can be large):
Used for: Sending messages, creating users, uploading files
content.explanation: GET sends data in the URL (limited space, visible to everyone). POST sends data in the request body (unlimited space, hidden). For AI chatbots, always use POST because messages can be very long.

content.title: Understanding Pydantic Models — Step by Step

sections.label: What is Pydantic?
sections.text: Pydantic is a Python library that checks if your data is correct. Think of it as a strict bouncer at a club — it checks your ID (data) before letting you in (processing).

sections.label: BaseModel
sections.text: Every Pydantic model inherits from BaseModel. It's like saying 'This class is an order form.' Any class that extends BaseModel gets automatic data validation.

sections.label: Type Hints
sections.text: 'message: str' means 'the message field MUST be a string.' If someone sends a number instead, Pydantic rejects it with a clear error message. No extra code needed!

sections.label: Default Values
sections.text: 'username: str = "Guest"' means 'username is optional. If not provided, use Guest as the default.' Fields WITHOUT defaults are required.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class UserProfile(BaseModel):
    name: str             # Required
    age: int              # Required, must be a number
    email: str            # Required
    is_premium: bool = False  # Optional, defaults to False

sections.label: Why This Matters
sections.text: Without Pydantic, you'd write 20 lines of 'if' statements to check every field. With Pydantic, you write 4 lines and FastAPI handles ALL the validation automatically. This saves you hours of work and prevents bugs.

POST is more secure because it encrypts data
questions.explanation: Chat messages can be very long. GET sends data in the URL (limited to ~2000 characters). POST sends data in the body (virtually unlimited size). That's why all chatbot APIs use POST.

content.title: Status Codes — The Server's Mood
content.explanation:
When you order food at a restaurant, the waiter might come back with different news:
- ✅ 'Here's your pizza!' (Everything went great!)
- 🤷 'Sorry, we don't have that item.' (What you asked for doesn't exist.)
- 🚫 'You need a reservation first.' (You're not allowed.)
- 💥 'The kitchen is on fire!' (Something went wrong on our side.)

Servers do the same thing using **Status Codes** — a number that tells the client what happened.

**The Main Status Codes You Need to Know:**

**2xx — SUCCESS (Everything is great!)**
• **200 OK** — 'Here's what you asked for!' (Most common success code)
• **201 Created** — 'Your new item was created successfully!'
• **202 Accepted** — 'Got your request, working on it in the background.'

**4xx — CLIENT ERROR (You made a mistake)**
• **400 Bad Request** — 'I don't understand what you sent me.'
• **401 Unauthorized** — 'Who are you? Show me your ID (login first).'
• **403 Forbidden** — 'I know who you are, but you don't have permission.'
• **404 Not Found** — 'That thing you asked for doesn't exist.'
• **422 Validation Error** — 'The data you sent is the wrong format.' (Very common with FastAPI/Pydantic)
• **429 Too Many Requests** — 'Slow down! You're sending too many requests.'

**5xx — SERVER ERROR (The server messed up)**
• **500 Internal Server Error** — 'Something went wrong on our end. Sorry!'
• **503 Service Unavailable** — 'The server is overloaded or down for maintenance.'
content.tip: Remember the pattern: 2xx = Success, 4xx = Client's fault (you sent something wrong), 5xx = Server's fault (something broke on our side). The most common ones are 200 (OK), 404 (Not Found), and 500 (Server Error).

stages.title: The Missing User
stages.description: You built an API endpoint GET /users/{user_id}. A client requests GET /users/999 but user 999 doesn't exist in your database. What should your server do?

choices.text: Return an empty response with status 200 OK
choices.outcome: Wrong! 200 means 'everything went great,' but the user wasn't found. This misleads the client.

choices.text: Return status 404 Not Found with a message: 'User 999 not found'
choices.outcome: Correct! 404 clearly tells the client 'what you asked for doesn't exist.' This is the proper way to handle missing resources.

choices.text: Return status 500 Internal Server Error
choices.outcome: Wrong! 500 means something broke on the server side. A missing user isn't a server error — it's a 'not found' situation (404).

content.title: Async & Await — Handling Multiple Customers at Once
content.explanation:
Imagine a restaurant with only ONE waiter. If a customer orders a dish that takes 30 minutes to cook, what does the waiter do?

**Bad Approach (Synchronous):**
The waiter stands at the kitchen door for 30 minutes waiting for the food. All other customers wait. Nobody gets served. 😡

**Good Approach (Asynchronous):**
The waiter takes the order to the kitchen, then IMMEDIATELY goes to serve other customers. When the food is ready, the waiter picks it up and delivers it. Meanwhile, everyone is being served. 🎉

**This is exactly what async/await does in Python!**

AI APIs are SLOW. When you send a message to OpenAI's API, it can take 2-30 seconds to respond. If your server has to WAIT for each AI response before helping the next user, only one person can use your app at a time!

**With async/await:**
- Your server sends the request to OpenAI
- Instead of waiting, it goes to help other users
- When OpenAI responds, it picks up the response and sends it back
- Result: hundreds of users can be served at the same time!

**The Code Difference:**

Regular function (synchronous — waiter stands and waits):
```python
def chat():  # ← regular function
    result = call_ai()  # blocks everything
    return result
```

Async function (asynchronous — waiter goes to help others):
```python
async def chat():  # ← async function
    result = await call_ai()  # lets server handle other requests while waiting
    return result
```

The ONLY difference is adding `async` before `def` and `await` before any slow operation. That's it!
content.example:
from fastapi import FastAPI
import asyncio

app = FastAPI()

# SYNCHRONOUS — Bad for slow tasks
# The server is STUCK while waiting
@app.get("/slow-sync")
def slow_sync():
    import time
    time.sleep(5)  # Server can't do ANYTHING for 5 seconds
    return {"message": "Done after 5 seconds"}

# ASYNCHRONOUS — Good for slow tasks  
# The server helps other users while waiting
@app.get("/slow-async")
async def slow_async():
    await asyncio.sleep(5)  # Server handles OTHER requests during these 5 seconds!
    return {"message": "Done after 5 seconds"}

# Real-world example: calling an AI API
# async def get_ai_response(message: str):
#     response = await openai_client.chat.completions.create(
#         model="gpt-4o",
#         messages=[{"role": "user", "content": message}]
#     )
#     return response.choices[0].message.content
content.tip: Rule of thumb: If your function calls any external service (AI APIs, databases, file reading), make it async. Add 'async' before 'def' and 'await' before the slow call. Your users will thank you!

content.title: Sync vs Async — The Restaurant Example

items.text: Imagine a restaurant with 100 customers but only 1 waiter.
SYNCHRONOUS waiter: Takes order from customer 1, stands at the kitchen for 10 minutes waiting, then serves customer 1, THEN goes to customer 2. After 100 customers, it takes 1000 minutes (16 hours)!

ASYNCHRONOUS waiter: Takes order from customer 1, sends it to kitchen, IMMEDIATELY goes to customer 2, takes their order, sends it to kitchen, goes to customer 3... When food is ready, picks it up and delivers it.
The async waiter serves all 100 customers in about 30 minutes instead of 16 hours. That's the power of async!

content.title: FastAPI vs Flask — Choosing Your Tool
content.explanation:
Before we go deeper, let's clearly understand why we're using FastAPI and not Flask. Both are Python web frameworks, but they're built for different eras.

**Flask — The Veteran (Born 2010):**

Flask has been around for 15+ years. It's simple, well-documented, and has a HUGE community. Millions of tutorials exist. BUT:
- It's **synchronous by default** — one slow request blocks everything
- **No built-in validation** — you manually check every field with if-statements
- **No auto-documentation** — you have to write API docs by hand
- Best for: simple websites, basic REST APIs, learning web development basics

**FastAPI — The Modern Choice (Born 2018):**

FastAPI was built specifically for the modern world of AI and real-time applications:
- It's **asynchronous by default** — handles many requests at once
- **Automatic validation** with Pydantic — no manual checking needed
- **Auto-generated docs** — beautiful interactive documentation at /docs
- **Type safety** — catches bugs before they happen
- Best for: AI backends, streaming APIs, high-performance applications

**When to Use What:**

| Feature | Flask | FastAPI |
|---------|-------|--------|
| Speed | Slower | 2-3x faster |
| Async support | Manual/difficult | Built-in |
| Data validation | Write yourself | Automatic (Pydantic) |
| API documentation | Write manually | Auto-generated |
| Learning curve | Easier | Slightly steeper |
| AI ecosystem fit | Poor | Perfect |

**Our choice: FastAPI** — because we're building AI applications where speed, validation, and streaming matter.

left.title: Flask
points: Synchronous by default — blocks on slow operations like AI API calls.
No built-in request validation — you manually check every field.
No auto-generated documentation — you write API docs by hand.
Massive ecosystem and community (older, more mature).
Best for: simple CRUD APIs, legacy systems, learning basics.

right.title: FastAPI
points: Async by default — handles hundreds of concurrent AI requests.
Automatic Pydantic validation on every request/response.
Auto-generated interactive OpenAPI (Swagger) documentation.
Purpose-built for modern APIs with type safety.
Best for: AI backends, streaming APIs, high-concurrency systems.

content.title: Streaming Responses — Why AI Feels Instant
content.explanation:
Have you noticed how ChatGPT shows words one by one, like someone is typing? That's not a fancy animation — that's **streaming**!

**The Problem Without Streaming:**

When you ask an AI a long question, the AI might take 10 seconds to generate the full answer. Without streaming:
1. You send your question
2. You stare at a loading spinner for 10 seconds
3. Suddenly, the entire answer appears at once

This feels SLOW and frustrating, even if the actual processing time is the same.

**The Solution With Streaming:**

With streaming, the server sends each word/token as it's generated:
1. You send your question
2. After 0.5 seconds: 'Python'
3. After 0.6 seconds: 'Python is'
4. After 0.7 seconds: 'Python is a'
5. ...words keep appearing one by one...
6. After 10 seconds: the full answer is complete

Same total time (10 seconds), but the user sees the first word in 0.5 seconds!

**How Streaming Works (Server-Sent Events / SSE):**

SSE is the technology behind streaming. Think of it like a live news ticker:
- The client opens a connection to the server
- The server sends small pieces of data one at a time through that connection
- Each piece starts with 'data: ' and ends with two newlines
- When done, the server sends a special 'DONE' signal

**In FastAPI:**

FastAPI uses something called a **generator function** — a special function that uses `yield` instead of `return`. Instead of building the whole response and returning it all at once, it yields (sends) one piece at a time.
content.tip: yield is like a return that doesn't stop the function. Regular return: 'Here's the whole answer, I'm done.' yield: 'Here's one piece, I have more coming.' The function pauses after each yield and continues when the next piece is needed.

content.title: Normal Response vs Streaming Response
diagram: User asks question → [Waiting... 10 seconds...] → Full answer appears at once
Time to see FIRST word: 10 seconds 😴
User asks question → 'The' → 'The answer' → 'The answer is' → ... → Complete!
Time to see FIRST word: 0.5 seconds ⚡
Total time is the SAME, but streaming FEELS much faster
content.explanation: Streaming doesn't make the AI faster — it makes the EXPERIENCE faster. Users start reading the answer immediately instead of staring at a loading spinner. This is why every AI chatbot (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) uses streaming.

sections.label: return
sections.text: A normal function uses 'return'. It gives you the ENTIRE answer at once and the function ENDS. Like a chef who cooks the ENTIRE meal and brings it all out at once.

sections.label: yield
sections.text: A generator function uses 'yield'. It gives you ONE PIECE at a time. After each yield, the function PAUSES (not ends). When you ask for the next piece, it continues from where it left off.

sections.label: Why yield for streaming?
sections.text: Streaming needs to send data piece by piece. 'yield' is perfect because it lets you send one word, pause, send the next word, pause, and so on — instead of waiting for the whole response.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# Regular function with return:
def get_all_words():
    return ['Hello', 'World']  # Everything at once

# Generator function with yield:
def get_words_one_by_one():
    yield 'Hello'  # Send first word, pause
    yield 'World'  # Send second word, pause

sections.label: SSE Format

challenge.title: Build a Streaming Countdown
challenge.hint: Use a for loop with range(5, 0, -1) to count down. Use yield with f-strings to format each number in SSE format: f"data: {number}\n\n"

content.title: Streaming AI Responses — The Real Thing
content.explanation:
Now let's combine everything we've learned and stream REAL AI responses! This is exactly how ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude work under the hood.

**The Flow:**
1. User sends a message to your server via POST /chat
2. Your server forwards the message to the AI provider (like OpenAI) with `stream=True`
3. The AI sends back tokens (words) one at a time
4. Your server immediately forwards each token to the user
5. The user sees words appearing in real-time!

**Key Concept — stream=True:**

When you call OpenAI's API normally, it waits until the ENTIRE response is generated, then sends it all at once. But when you add `stream=True`, it sends each token (word/piece) as it's generated.

**The SSE Format for AI Streaming:**
```
data: {"text": "Hello"}

data: {"text": " there"}

data: {"text": "!"}

data: [DONE]
```

Each chunk is a JSON object wrapped in the SSE format. The client parses each chunk and appends the text to the screen.
content.example:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel
import json

app = FastAPI()

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    message: str

# Simulated AI streaming (without needing an actual API key)
def fake_ai_stream(message: str):
    """Simulates an AI streaming response word by word."""
    import time
    response_words = f"Great question! You asked about: {message}. Let me explain in detail.".split(" ")
    
    for word in response_words:
        chunk = json.dumps({"text": word + " "})
        yield f"data: {chunk}\n\n"
        time.sleep(0.2)
    
    yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"

@app.post("/chat/stream")
def stream_chat(request: ChatRequest):
    return StreamingResponse(
        fake_ai_stream(request.message),
        media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={"Cache-Control": "no-cache"}  # Don't cache the stream!
    )

# With a REAL AI API (like OpenAI), it would look like this:
# def real_ai_stream(message: str):
#     from openai import OpenAI
#     client = OpenAI()
#     stream = client.chat.completions.create(
#         model="gpt-4o",
#         messages=[{"role": "user", "content": message}],
#         stream=True  # ← This is the magic flag!
#     )
#     for chunk in stream:
#         content = chunk.choices[0].delta.content
#         if content:
#             yield f"data: {json.dumps({'text': content})}\n\n"
#     yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"
content.tip: When using OpenAI's real API, the ONLY change is adding stream=True to the API call. Everything else (the SSE format, the generator, the StreamingResponse) stays exactly the same!

content.title: WebSockets — Real-Time Two-Way Chat
content.explanation:
SSE (Server-Sent Events) is great for one-way streaming (server → client). But what if you want TRUE real-time conversation where BOTH sides can send messages at ANY time?

**The Phone Call Analogy:**

- **REST API** = Sending a letter. You write a letter (request), mail it, wait for a reply (response), then write another letter. Very slow.
- **SSE** = Listening to the radio. The station (server) broadcasts, and you listen. But you can't talk back through the radio.
- **WebSocket** = A phone call. Both sides can talk AND listen at the same time. No waiting turns!

**When to Use What:**

| Technology | Direction | Best For |
|------------|-----------|----------|
| REST (GET/POST) | Client → Server → Client | Simple Q&A, one-time requests |
| SSE | Server → Client (one way) | AI text streaming, live updates |
| WebSocket | Both ways at same time | Real-time chat, collaborative editing, voice |

**How WebSockets Work in FastAPI:**

1. The client opens a WebSocket connection (like calling a phone number)
2. The server accepts the connection (picks up the phone)
3. Both sides can send messages at any time
4. The connection stays open until one side hangs up

This is perfect for chat applications where the user types a message, the AI responds in real-time, and the user can type another message before the AI even finishes!
content.example:
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket

app = FastAPI()

@app.websocket("/ws/chat")
async def websocket_chat(websocket: WebSocket):
    # Step 1: Accept the connection (pick up the phone)
    await websocket.accept()
    print("Client connected!")
    
    # Step 2: Keep the conversation going
    while True:
        try:
            # Wait for the client to send a message
            user_message = await websocket.receive_text()
            print(f"User said: {user_message}")
            
            # Send a response back
            reply = f"You said: '{user_message}' — I heard you loud and clear!"
            await websocket.send_text(reply)
            
        except Exception:
            # Client disconnected (hung up the phone)
            print("Client disconnected.")
            break

# To test this, you'd need a WebSocket client.
# The simplest way is to use the /docs page or JavaScript:
# const ws = new WebSocket('ws://localhost:8000/ws/chat');
# ws.onmessage = (event) => console.log(event.data);
# ws.send('Hello!');
content.tip: Use REST for simple requests. Use SSE for one-way AI streaming. Use WebSockets when you need a continuous, two-way conversation. Most AI chatbots use SSE because the user sends one message and the AI streams one response back.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of streaming AI responses?
options: It makes the AI model smarter
It reduces the total response time
The user sees the first word almost immediately instead of waiting for the full response
questions.explanation: Streaming doesn't change the total time — the AI takes the same time. But the user sees the FIRST word in under a second, making the experience feel much faster.

questions.question: What Python keyword is used to send one piece of data at a time in a generator function?
questions.explanation: 'yield' sends one piece of data at a time without ending the function. The function pauses after each yield and continues when the next piece is needed.

questions.question: What does SSE stand for?
questions.explanation: SSE stands for Server-Sent Events — a technology where the server pushes data to the client over an open HTTP connection.

questions.question: When should you use WebSockets instead of SSE?
options: When you only need the server to send data
When both client AND server need to send messages at any time
When you have more than 10 users
questions.explanation: WebSockets provide bidirectional communication — both sides can send messages at any time. SSE is only server → client.

content.title: Authentication — Locking the Door to Your API
content.explanation:
Imagine you built an amazing AI chatbot API. Each AI response costs you $0.01. Now imagine someone discovers your API and starts sending 1 million requests. That's $10,000 gone in minutes!

**Authentication is like a bouncer at a club.** Before anyone can use your API, they need to prove who they are.

**The Three Questions of Security:**
1. **Authentication** = 'WHO are you?' (Proving your identity — showing your ID)
2. **Authorization** = 'WHAT are you allowed to do?' (Checking your permissions — VIP vs regular)
3. **Rate Limiting** = 'HOW MUCH can you use?' (Setting limits — max 2 drinks per hour)

**API Keys — The Simplest Lock:**

An API key is like a house key — a secret string that you give to trusted users. They include it in every request to prove they have permission.

You've probably already used API keys! When you use the OpenAI API, you need an API key like `sk-abc123...`. Without it, OpenAI won't respond to your requests.

**JWT (JSON Web Tokens) — The Smart ID Card:**

JWTs are more advanced than API keys. A JWT is like a smart ID card that contains information INSIDE it:
- Who you are (user ID, email)
- What you're allowed to do (admin, regular user)
- When it expires (after 1 hour)
- A tamper-proof seal (digital signature)

The beauty of JWTs is that the server doesn't need to look anything up in a database — all the info is right there in the token. It just needs to verify the signature to make sure nobody tampered with it.
content.tip: API keys are simple but powerful. Always send them in headers (like 'X-API-Key'), never in the URL. Anyone who sees the URL (in logs, browser history) could steal your key!

content.title: JWT (JSON Web Tokens) — How Login Works
content.explanation:
API keys work great for machine-to-machine communication, but for human users (like people logging into your AI app), we use **JWT (JSON Web Tokens)**.

**The Login Flow — Step by Step:**

**Step 1: User Logs In**
- User sends username + password to your server
- Server checks if they're correct
- If correct, server creates a JWT token and sends it back

**Step 2: User Makes Requests**
- For every future request, the user includes the JWT token
- Server checks the token to verify the user's identity
- No need to send username/password again!

**Step 3: Token Expires**
- After some time (e.g., 24 hours), the token expires
- User needs to log in again to get a new token

**What's Inside a JWT?**

A JWT has three parts, separated by dots:
`eyJhbGciOi...`.`eyJzdWIiOi...`.`SflKxwRJSM...`

1. **Header** — The algorithm used (e.g., HS256)
2. **Payload** — The actual data (user_id, email, expiration time)
3. **Signature** — A mathematical proof that nobody tampered with the token

The payload is NOT encrypted — anyone can read it. But they can't CHANGE it, because the signature would no longer match. Think of it like a sealed envelope — you can see through it, but you can't change what's inside without breaking the seal.
content.tip: The JWT workflow: Login → Get Token → Send Token with every request → Server verifies Token → Access granted. The token is like a wristband at a festival — show it once to get in, then flash it to access different areas.

content.title: Rate Limiting — Don't Let Anyone Bankrupt You
content.explanation:
Even with authentication, you have a problem. What if a valid user sends 10,000 requests per minute? Each AI request costs money. Without limits, one user could drain your entire budget!

**Rate Limiting = Setting a Speed Limit**

Just like roads have speed limits to keep everyone safe, APIs have rate limits to keep your server (and your wallet) safe.

**How Rate Limiting Works:**

1. You decide: 'Each user can make 10 requests per minute'
2. The server keeps count of each user's requests
3. If they hit the limit, the server returns **429 Too Many Requests**
4. After the time window resets, they can make requests again

**Real-World Examples:**
- OpenAI: Free tier = 3 requests/minute, Paid = 3,500 requests/minute
- Twitter/X API: 1,500 tweets/month on free tier
- Google Maps: 28,500 requests/day on free tier

**The Sliding Window Algorithm:**

Instead of resetting the count every minute on the dot (which can cause bursts), we use a 'sliding window' — we look at the last 60 seconds from right NOW. If there are too many requests in that window, reject the new one.
content.tip: HTTP 429 is the standard status code for 'Too Many Requests.' When you receive a 429, you should wait and retry later. Most well-behaved clients (and libraries) handle this automatically.

choices.outcome: This punishes legitimate users too and doesn't actually prevent the abuse. The attacker can still send 50,000 slow requests.

content.title: Middleware — The Security Guard at Every Door
content.explanation:
Imagine a building where every room has its own security guard checking IDs. That's wasteful! Instead, you put ONE security guard at the main entrance who checks everyone before they enter ANY room.

**That's what Middleware does.**

Middleware is code that runs on EVERY single request BEFORE it reaches your endpoint function, and on EVERY response BEFORE it goes back to the client.

**Why Middleware?**

Instead of adding logging, authentication, and timing code to every single endpoint (copy-pasting the same code 50 times), you write it ONCE as middleware and it automatically applies to everything.

**Common Uses for Middleware:**

1. **CORS** — Allowing your frontend (running on localhost:3000) to talk to your backend (running on localhost:8000). Without CORS, the browser blocks cross-origin requests.

2. **Request Timing** — Measuring how long each request takes. Useful for finding slow endpoints.

3. **Logging** — Recording every request (who asked, what they asked, when they asked).

4. **Error Handling** — Catching crashes and returning a clean error instead of showing ugly internal error messages.

5. **Rate Limiting** — Checking request counts before any endpoint runs (as we just learned!).
content.example:
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
import time

app = FastAPI()

# --- Middleware 1: CORS (Allow frontend to talk to backend) ---
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["http://localhost:3000"],  # Your frontend URL
    allow_methods=["*"],  # Allow all HTTP methods
    allow_headers=["*"],  # Allow all headers
)

# --- Middleware 2: Request Timer ---
@app.middleware("http")
async def add_timing(request: Request, call_next):
    start_time = time.time()
    
    response = await call_next(request)  # Let the request go through
    
    process_time = time.time() - start_time
    response.headers["X-Process-Time"] = str(round(process_time, 4))
    print(f"{request.method} {request.url.path} took {process_time:.4f}s")
    
    return response

# --- Your normal endpoints ---
@app.get("/")
def home():
    return {"message": "Hello!"}

@app.get("/slow")
async def slow_endpoint():
    import asyncio
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    return {"message": "This was slow!"}

# Every request will now show timing in the console:
# GET / took 0.0012s
# GET /slow took 2.0034s
content.tip: CORS is the #1 thing beginners struggle with. If your frontend gets 'CORS error', it means you forgot to add CORSMiddleware to your FastAPI app. The example above shows exactly how to fix it!

content.title: Background Tasks — Don't Make the Customer Wait
content.explanation:
Some tasks take a LONG time. Imagine you're building an AI that:
- Researches a topic by reading 50 websites (takes 5 minutes)
- Generates a 10-page report (takes 3 minutes)
- Sends the report via email

You can't make the user stare at a loading screen for 8 minutes! That's terrible UX.

**The Solution — Background Tasks:**

1. User sends request: 'Generate a report on climate change'
2. Server says: 'Got it! Here's your job ID: abc123. I'll work on it in the background.'
3. Server returns immediately (in under 1 second)
4. The long task runs in the background
5. User can check the status: GET /jobs/abc123 → 'Still working... 60% done'
6. When done: GET /jobs/abc123 → 'Complete! Here's your report.'

**FastAPI has built-in BackgroundTasks:**

For simple tasks (sending an email, saving a log), FastAPI has a built-in BackgroundTasks feature. You add a task to the background, and it runs after the response is sent.

**For heavy tasks, use Celery:**

For serious work (running AI models, processing large files), you need **Celery** — a task queue that runs tasks on separate worker processes. Think of it as hiring extra kitchen staff to handle big orders while the main kitchen keeps taking new orders.
content.tip: The key pattern: POST to start a job → get a job_id back immediately → GET to check status later. This is how every professional API handles long-running tasks (GitHub Actions, AWS, Google Cloud — they all use this pattern).

content.explanation: Background tasks let you handle long-running operations without making the user wait. The user gets an immediate response with a job ID, and can check back later for the result.

content.explanation:
Let's combine EVERYTHING we've learned into one complete AI backend application. This is what a real-world AI chatbot backend looks like!

**Our App Has:**
1. ✅ A health check endpoint (GET /health)
2. ✅ A chat endpoint with Pydantic validation (POST /chat)

4. ✅ API key authentication

This is a production-ready foundation. Every AI startup begins with something like this!

content.title: Dependency Injection — Keeping Your Code Clean
content.explanation:
As your app grows, you'll notice you're writing the same code over and over. For example, every protected endpoint needs to verify the API key. FastAPI has a genius solution: **Dependency Injection** with `Depends()`.

**The Problem:**
```python
@app.get("/endpoint1")
def endpoint1(x_api_key: str = Header()):
    user = verify_key(x_api_key)  # Same code repeated!
    ...

@app.get("/endpoint2")
def endpoint2(x_api_key: str = Header()):
    user = verify_key(x_api_key)  # Same code repeated again!
    ...
```

**The Solution — Depends():**
```python
@app.get("/endpoint1")
def endpoint1(user: str = Depends(verify_key)):
    # 'user' is automatically the result of verify_key()!
    ...
```

`Depends()` tells FastAPI: 'Before running this endpoint, run this other function first. Give me the result as a parameter.'

This is incredibly powerful because:
1. You write the verification logic ONCE
2. You reuse it in EVERY endpoint with just `Depends(verify_key)`
3. For testing, you can easily swap out the real function with a fake one
4. FastAPI handles all the plumbing for you
content.tip: Depends() is like hiring one receptionist for the whole building instead of putting a guard in every room. Write once, use everywhere. It's one of FastAPI's most powerful features.

content.title: Project Structure — Organizing a Real Application
content.explanation:
When your API grows from 5 endpoints to 50 endpoints, having everything in one file becomes messy. Let's organize our code like a professional!

**Small Project (1 file):**
```
my_app/
├── main.py          # Everything in one file
└── requirements.txt # Dependencies
```

**Medium Project (multiple files):**
```
my_app/
├── main.py           # App setup, middleware, startup
├── routes/
│   ├── chat.py       # /chat endpoints
│   ├── auth.py       # /login, /register endpoints
│   └── health.py     # /health endpoint
├── models/
│   └── schemas.py    # Pydantic models (ChatRequest, etc.)
├── services/
│   └── ai_service.py # Business logic (calling OpenAI, etc.)
├── dependencies/
│   └── auth.py       # Depends() functions
└── requirements.txt
```

**The Key Idea — Separation of Concerns:**
Each file has ONE job:
- **routes/** = What endpoints exist and what they accept
- **models/** = What data looks like (Pydantic models)
- **services/** = The actual logic (calling AI, processing data)
- **dependencies/** = Shared stuff (auth, database connections)

FastAPI uses `APIRouter` to split routes across files. Each file creates its own router, and `main.py` includes them all.
content.example:
# ===== routes/chat.py =====
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends
from models.schemas import ChatRequest
from services.ai_service import get_ai_response
from dependencies.auth import get_current_user

router = APIRouter(prefix="/chat", tags=["Chat"])

@router.post("/")
def chat(request: ChatRequest, user: str = Depends(get_current_user)):
    response = get_ai_response(request.message)
    return {"user": user, "reply": response}

# ===== models/schemas.py =====
from pydantic import BaseModel

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    message: str
    model: str = "gpt-4o-mini"

# ===== services/ai_service.py =====
def get_ai_response(message: str) -> str:
    return f"AI response to: {message}"

# ===== main.py =====
from fastapi import FastAPI
from routes.chat import router as chat_router

app = FastAPI(title="My AI API")
app.include_router(chat_router)  # Include all /chat routes
content.tip: Start with one file. When it grows past 200 lines, split it into multiple files. Don't over-engineer from day one — let the structure grow naturally with your project.

content.title: Deploying Your API — Going Live!
content.explanation:
Right now, your API only works on your laptop (localhost). To let other people use it, you need to **deploy** it — put it on a computer that's always on and connected to the internet.

**The Deployment Stack:**

1. **Uvicorn** = The engine that runs your FastAPI app. Like the engine in a car.
2. **Gunicorn** = The driver that manages multiple Uvicorn engines. For production, you want multiple workers (engines) running at the same time.
3. **Docker** = A container that packages your app + all its dependencies so it runs the same everywhere. Like a shipping container — doesn't matter if it's on a ship, train, or truck.
4. **Cloud Platform** = Where your Docker container actually runs. Options:
   - **Railway / Render** — Easiest for beginners (just connect GitHub)
   - **AWS / Google Cloud / Azure** — For professional, large-scale apps
   - **Vercel** — Great if combined with a frontend

**The Production Command:**

Development (your laptop): `uvicorn main:app --reload`
Production (real server): `gunicorn main:app -w 4 -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker`

The `-w 4` means '4 workers' — 4 copies of your app running at the same time to handle more users.

**Health Check Endpoints:**

Every production API needs a health check — a simple endpoint that says 'I'm alive!' Cloud platforms use this to know if your server is healthy or if it needs to restart it.
content.example:
# main.py — Production-Ready FastAPI App
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI(title="My AI API", version="1.0.0")

# Health check — cloud platforms ping this to check if server is alive
@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "healthy"}

@app.get("/")
def root():
    return {"message": "Welcome to my AI API! Visit /docs for documentation."}

# ----- Dockerfile -----
# Create a file called 'Dockerfile' (no extension):
#
# FROM python:3.11-slim
# WORKDIR /app
# COPY requirements.txt .
# RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
# COPY . .
# CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

# ----- requirements.txt -----
# fastapi
# uvicorn

# ----- Run locally -----
# uvicorn main:app --reload

# ----- Run in production -----
# gunicorn main:app -w 4 -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker --bind 0.0.0.0:8000
content.tip: Start with Railway or Render for your first deployment — they're free and you can deploy by just connecting your GitHub repository. As you grow, move to Docker + AWS/GCP.

content.title: Database Architecture for AI Applications
content.explanation: AI applications require a layered database strategy. No single database handles everything — you need relational databases for structured data, document databases for flexible schemas, and in-memory stores for caching and real-time performance.

content.title: The Three-Layer Database Strategy
content.body: Layer 1: PostgreSQL for structured, relational data (users, subscriptions, chat sessions). Layer 2: MongoDB for semi-structured data (flexible message formats, agent logs). Layer 3: Redis for ephemeral, high-speed data (caching, rate limiting, session state).

content.title: PostgreSQL: The Backbone
content.body: The most powerful open-source relational database. ACID-compliant, supports complex queries, JSON columns, full-text search, and — critically — the pgvector extension that turns PostgreSQL into a vector database for RAG.

content.title: pgvector: Vector Search in PostgreSQL
content.body: The pgvector extension adds vector data types and similarity search operators to PostgreSQL. Store your embeddings alongside your relational data. No need for a separate vector database — one PostgreSQL instance handles both structured queries AND semantic search.

content.title: MongoDB: Flexible Document Store
content.body: MongoDB stores data as JSON-like documents with no fixed schema. Perfect for AI applications where data structures evolve rapidly — agent execution logs, varied tool outputs, multi-format chat messages (text, images, files).

content.title: Redis: The Speed Layer
content.body: An in-memory key-value store with sub-millisecond latency. Use for: LLM response caching (same question = cached answer, saving token costs), rate limiting counters, session state, real-time agent state during execution.

content.title: Caching Strategy for LLMs
content.body:
Cache at multiple levels:

1. Exact match — hash the prompt, cache the response.

2. Semantic cache — embed the prompt, find similar cached prompts within a threshold.

3. Prefix cache — cache common system prompt prefixes. Redis handles levels 1 and 3; pgvector handles level 2.

content.title: Data Modeling for Chat
content.body: A typical chat schema: Users table → has many Conversations → has many Messages. Each Message has: role (system/user/assistant/tool), content, token_count, model_used, latency_ms, cost_usd. This enables both conversation replay and cost analytics.

blocks.content:
```python
import psycopg2

conn = psycopg2.connect("postgresql://user:pass@localhost/aidb")
cur = conn.cursor()

cur.execute("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;")

cur.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS documents (
        id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
        content TEXT NOT NULL,
        embedding vector(1536),
        metadata JSONB,
        created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
    );
""")

cur.execute("""
    CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS docs_embedding_idx 
    ON documents USING ivfflat (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
    WITH (lists = 100);
""")

conn.commit()
```

content.title: Vector Databases Overview
content.explanation: Vector databases are purpose-built to store, index, and search high-dimensional embedding vectors at scale. They are the backbone of every RAG pipeline, semantic search engine, and recommendation system. Unlike traditional databases that match exact values, vector databases find the 'most similar' items using distance metrics like cosine similarity. Choosing the right vector database is one of the most consequential architectural decisions in an AI application.

content.title: Pinecone
content.body: Fully managed, serverless vector database. Zero operational overhead — no servers to provision, no indexes to tune. Supports metadata filtering, namespaces for multi-tenancy, and sparse-dense hybrid search. Pricing: pay per vector stored + per query. Best for: teams that want zero ops overhead and are okay with vendor lock-in. Limitation: closed-source, data is stored on Pinecone's infrastructure.

content.title: Qdrant
content.body: Open-source, written in Rust for maximum performance. Supports filtering, payload indexing, and advanced distance metrics. Can run locally (Docker), self-hosted, or as a managed cloud service. Features binary quantization for 40x faster search with minimal quality loss. Best for: teams that need high performance, open-source flexibility, and self-hosting capability.

content.title: Weaviate
content.body: Open-source, written in Go. Unique feature: built-in vectorization modules — you can insert raw text and Weaviate automatically embeds it using a configured model (no separate embedding pipeline needed). Supports GraphQL-like query syntax, multi-modal search (text + images), and hybrid BM25+vector search natively. Best for: teams that want an all-in-one solution with minimal pipeline complexity.

content.title: Milvus
content.body: Open-source, designed for billion-scale deployments. Supports multiple index types (IVF, HNSW, DiskANN) with fine-grained tuning. Runs as a distributed cluster with separate storage and compute layers. GPU-accelerated search for massive throughput. Best for: enterprises with billions of vectors that need horizontal scalability and are willing to manage the operational complexity.

content.title: pgvector (PostgreSQL Extension)
content.body: Adds vector storage and similarity search to your existing PostgreSQL database. No separate infrastructure needed — your vectors live alongside your relational data. Supports HNSW and IVFFlat indexes. Performance is good up to ~5M vectors; beyond that, dedicated vector databases are faster. Best for: teams already using PostgreSQL who want to avoid adding another database to their stack.

content.title: ChromaDB
content.body: The simplest vector database to get started with. Runs in-memory or with SQLite persistence. Python-first API with a single `pip install chromadb`. No server setup required — just import and use. Best for: prototyping, local development, and small-scale applications (<100K vectors). Not recommended for production workloads requiring high availability or horizontal scaling.

content.title: Selection Criteria
content.body:
Choose based on:

1. Scale — how many vectors? <1M → pgvector/Chroma, 1-100M → Qdrant/Weaviate/Pinecone, 1B+ → Milvus.
2. Ops budget — managed (Pinecone) vs self-hosted (Qdrant/Milvus).
3. Existing stack — already on Postgres? Start with pgvector.
4. Features — need hybrid search? Weaviate/Qdrant. Need built-in vectorization? Weaviate.
5. Budget — Pinecone costs scale with usage; self-hosted costs are fixed.

content.title: GraphRAG & Knowledge Graphs
content.explanation: Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) uses flat semantic vectors to find document text, often missing global relationships. GraphRAG integrates structured Knowledge Graphs to enable complex, multi-hop reasoning across interconnected documents.

content.title: Beyond Flat Vector Search
content.body: Standard vector databases search for independent text chunks using cosine similarity. While excellent for localized lookups, vector search cannot resolve structured relationships or answer global questions like 'Summarize the primary connections between Entity A and Entity B'.

content.title: What is a Knowledge Graph?
content.body: A Knowledge Graph stores information as entities (nodes) connected by explicit relationships (edges), represented as triples: (Subject, Predicate, Object) such as (CompanyA, acquired, CompanyB). This structures the data semantically.

content.title: Multi-Hop Reasoning
content.body: Knowledge Graphs allow agents to traverse connected nodes (hops) to answer queries requiring multi-layered facts. For example: finding CompanyA's CEO, checking their board memberships, and retrieving the related patent records.

content.title: Graph Databases: Neo4j
content.body: Neo4j is the industry standard native graph database. It uses Cypher, a graph query language, to retrieve structured relationships. AI backends query Neo4j to build rich, connected context before executing LLM reasoning steps.

content.title: Hybrid Search: Lexical + Vector + Graph
content.body: State-of-the-art RAG pipelines merge multiple search systems: BM25 (keyword matching), vector search (semantic similarity), and Graph query relationships. This hybrid approach ensures high precision and completeness.

content.title: Community Summarization
content.body: GraphRAG algorithms cluster related entities into 'communities' and generate hierarchal summary documents. When a user asks a global question, the system queries community summaries instead of doing hundreds of individual document retrieves.

content.title: Knowledge Graph Construction
content.body: Constructing graphs typically uses an LLM to parse text documents, extract entities and relationships, resolve coreferences, and build structured cypher queries to populate Neo4j database models automatically.

content.title: Vector Search Internals: HNSW & Approximate Nearest Neighbors
content.explanation: Vector databases power semantic search in RAG systems, but understanding how they actually find similar vectors is critical for tuning performance. HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the dominant algorithm behind pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate, and most production vector stores.

content.title: Exact vs Approximate Search
content.body: Exact nearest neighbor search compares the query vector against every stored vector (brute force). This is O(n) — for 10 million vectors, it is unusably slow. Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) algorithms trade a tiny accuracy loss for 1000x speed improvement, returning the 'approximately' closest vectors.

content.title: How HNSW Works
content.body: HNSW builds a multi-layer graph of vectors. The top layer is sparse (long-distance jumps for fast navigation). Each lower layer adds more connections (finer-grained search). At query time, the algorithm starts at the top layer, greedily navigates to the closest node, then drops down a layer for more precise search — like zooming in on a map.

content.title: Key HNSW Parameters
content.body: M (max connections per node): Higher M = better recall but more memory. ef_construction (search width during build): Higher = better index quality but slower build. ef_search (search width at query time): Higher = better recall but slower queries. Typical starting values: M=16, ef_construction=64, ef_search=40.

content.title: IVF-Flat: The Alternative
content.body: Inverted File Index (IVF) partitions vectors into clusters using k-means. At query time, only the nearest clusters are searched. IVF uses less memory than HNSW but has lower recall. pgvector supports both HNSW and IVF indexes — use HNSW for quality-critical RAG and IVF for memory-constrained environments.

content.title: Distance Metrics
content.body: Cosine similarity: measures the angle between vectors (most common for text embeddings). Euclidean distance (L2): measures straight-line distance. Inner product (dot product): measures magnitude-weighted similarity. Choose based on how your embedding model was trained — most text models use cosine.

content.title: Index Build Time vs Query Time
content.body: HNSW indexes are expensive to build (minutes to hours for millions of vectors) but extremely fast to query (<10ms). Plan for index rebuild time when adding large batches of new documents. Use incremental insertion for real-time document ingestion — HNSW supports adding vectors without full rebuild.

content.title: Recall-Latency Tradeoff
content.body: The fundamental tradeoff: higher ef_search = better recall (finding the true nearest neighbors) but higher latency. For RAG applications, 95% recall at 5ms is usually better than 99.9% recall at 50ms. Profile your specific workload to find the sweet spot.

```python
import numpy as np
import hnswlib

dim = 128
num_elements = 10000
data = np.random.rand(num_elements, dim).astype('float32')

index = hnswlib.Index(space='cosine', dim=dim)
index.init_index(
    max_elements=num_elements,
    ef_construction=200,
    M=16
)

index.add_items(data, ids=list(range(num_elements)))

index.set_ef(50)
query = np.random.rand(1, dim).astype('float32')
labels, distances = index.knn_query(query, k=5)
print(f"Top 5 nearest neighbors: {labels[0]}")
```

content.title: Hybrid Search
content.explanation: Neither semantic search nor keyword search alone is sufficient for production RAG systems. Semantic search excels at understanding intent ('ways to fix a broken pipe' matches 'plumbing repair guide') but fails at exact matches ('error code ERR-7842'). Keyword search (BM25) excels at exact matches but misses synonyms and paraphrases. Hybrid search combines both approaches, giving you the best of both worlds — and it's now considered a best practice for any serious RAG deployment.

content.title: Dense Retrieval (Semantic Search)
content.body: Convert the query and all documents into embedding vectors using a bi-encoder model. Find the most similar documents using cosine similarity or dot product. Strengths: understands paraphrases, handles synonyms, captures intent. Weaknesses: terrible at matching specific identifiers (serial numbers, error codes, proper nouns), can return semantically similar but factually wrong results.

content.title: Sparse Retrieval (BM25)
content.body: BM25 (Best Matching 25) is a keyword-based ranking algorithm that scores documents based on term frequency and inverse document frequency. No neural network involved — pure statistics. Strengths: exact keyword matching, handles rare vocabulary, deterministic and explainable. Weaknesses: misses synonyms ('car' won't match 'automobile'), doesn't understand context or intent.

content.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
content.body: RRF is the standard algorithm for merging results from two or more ranked lists into a single, optimized list. Formula: `score(d) = Σ(1 / (k + rank(d)))` where k=60 (constant) and rank(d) is the document's position in each source list. Documents that appear high in multiple lists get boosted. RRF is simple, effective, and parameter-free — it's the default fusion method in most production systems.

content.title: Weighted Combination
content.body: An alternative to RRF: normalize scores from each retriever to [0,1] and combine with weights: `final_score = α × dense_score + (1-α) × sparse_score`. The weight α controls the balance — start with α=0.7 (favoring semantic) and tune based on evaluation. More configurable than RRF but requires careful tuning per dataset.

content.title: SPLADE (Sparse Embedding)
content.body: A learned sparse retrieval model that bridges the gap between dense and sparse. SPLADE uses a trained model to generate sparse vectors with expanded vocabulary — it learns to add related terms that aren't in the original text. This gives BM25-like exact matching with neural-network-quality understanding. Used in production by Pinecone and Qdrant as their sparse retrieval backbone.

content.title: Implementation Patterns
content.body:
Two main architectures:

1. Parallel retrieval — run dense and sparse searches simultaneously, then fuse results. Requires maintaining two indexes.
2. Native hybrid — some databases (Weaviate, Qdrant, Elasticsearch) support hybrid search natively, handling both indexes and fusion internally. Native hybrid is simpler but less configurable. Parallel retrieval gives you full control over each component.

content.title: When to Use Hybrid vs Dense-Only
content.body:
Always use hybrid when:

1. Your documents contain specific identifiers (product codes, error numbers, legal citations).
2. Users mix natural language with exact terms.
3. You need maximum recall. Use dense-only when:

1. All queries are natural language with no exact-match requirements.
2. Simplicity and lower infrastructure cost are priorities.
3. Your evaluation shows negligible improvement from adding BM25.

blocks.content:
```python
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi
import numpy as np

documents = [
    "Python is great for machine learning",
    "JavaScript is popular for web development",
    "TensorFlow and PyTorch are deep learning frameworks",
]

tokenized = [doc.lower().split() for doc in documents]
bm25 = BM25Okapi(tokenized)
bm25_scores = bm25.get_scores("python machine learning".split())

vector_scores = np.array([0.85, 0.30, 0.72])

def rrf_score(keyword_rank, vector_rank, k=60):
    return 1/(k + keyword_rank) + 1/(k + vector_rank)

keyword_ranks = np.argsort(-bm25_scores)
vector_ranks = np.argsort(-vector_scores)

for i, doc in enumerate(documents):
    kr = np.where(keyword_ranks == i)[0][0]
    vr = np.where(vector_ranks == i)[0][0]
    print(f"Doc {i}: RRF={rrf_score(kr, vr):.4f} | {doc[:50]}")
```

content.title: Querying pgvector in Code
content.explanation: Once your embeddings are stored in PostgreSQL, you use the pgvector extension's custom SQL operators to perform similarity searches directly alongside your standard relational queries.

content.title: The Vector Type
content.body: In your database schema, embedding columns are defined with the `vector(DIMENSIONS)` type. For example, OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small requires a `vector(1536)` column.

content.title: The Cosine Distance Operator (<=>)
content.body: pgvector introduces new operators. The most common is `<=>`, which calculates Cosine Distance. To find the similarity between a stored embedding and a query vector, you use: `embedding <=> '[0.1, 0.2, ...]'`.

content.title: Ordering by Similarity
content.body: To perform a semantic search, you ORDER BY the cosine distance ascending (lowest distance = highest similarity) and use a LIMIT clause. Example: `ORDER BY embedding <=> query_vector LIMIT 5`.

content.title: Hybrid Search
content.body: The true power of pgvector is mixing vector search with standard SQL filters. You can filter by a specific user ID before sorting by similarity: `WHERE user_id = 5 ORDER BY embedding <=> query_vector LIMIT 3`.

content.title: Putting It All Together
content.body:
Here is the complete code. Notice how all the components come together:

```sql
SELECT content 
FROM messages 
WHERE user_id = 123 
ORDER BY embedding <=> :query_vector 
LIMIT 3;
```

content.example:
-- Standard PostgreSQL query with pgvector extension
-- The <-> operator computes the L2 distance between vectors
SELECT id, text_content, embedding <-> '[0.11, 0.24, 0.55, 0.81]' AS distance
FROM documents
ORDER BY distance ASC
LIMIT 5;

content.question: Match each database to its ideal use case in AI applications.

content.title: Project: AI Chat History System
content.explanation: A production chat history system must store conversations persistently, enable fast retrieval, support semantic search over past messages, and provide analytics on usage and cost.

content.title: Schema Design
content.body: PostgreSQL tables: users (id, email, plan), conversations (id, user_id, title, created_at), messages (id, conversation_id, role, content, token_count, model, latency_ms, cost_usd, embedding vector(1536), created_at).

content.title: Message Storage Flow
content.body:
When a user sends a message:

1. Store the user message in PostgreSQL.

2. Generate the embedding and store it in the embedding column.

3. Send to LLM.

4. Stream the response tokens to the user.

5. Store the complete assistant message with metadata (tokens, cost, latency).

content.title: Semantic Search
content.body: When the user asks 'What did we discuss about pricing last week?', embed the query, and use pgvector's cosine similarity search to find the most relevant past messages across all their conversations.

content.title: Redis Caching Layer
content.body: Cache the last 50 messages of active conversations in Redis for instant loading. When a user opens a conversation, serve from Redis (sub-ms) instead of PostgreSQL (5-10ms). Expire cache entries after 1 hour of inactivity.

content.title: Conversation Summarization
content.body: When a conversation exceeds 50 messages, trigger a background job that summarizes the conversation using a small LLM. Store the summary in the conversations table. Use the summary for context when loading long conversation threads.

content.title: Analytics Dashboard
content.body:
Query PostgreSQL to build:

1. Daily active users

2. Total tokens consumed per day

3. Average response latency

4. Cost per user per month

5. Most popular topics (via embedding clustering).

content.title: Data Retention & Privacy
content.body: Implement configurable data retention policies. Users can delete their chat history (GDPR right to erasure). Encrypt messages at rest using AES-256. Use row-level security in PostgreSQL so users can only access their own data.

```python
import psycopg2

conn = psycopg2.connect("postgresql://user:pass@localhost/chatdb")
cur = conn.cursor()

cur.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (
        id UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() PRIMARY KEY,
        conversation_id UUID,
        role TEXT NOT NULL,
        content TEXT NOT NULL,
        embedding vector(1536),
        created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
    );
""")

def save_message(conversation_id, role, content, embedding=None):
    cur.execute(
        "INSERT INTO messages (conversation_id, role, content, embedding) VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s)",
        (conversation_id, role, content, embedding)
    )
    conn.commit()

def search_history(query_embedding, limit=5):
    cur.execute("""
        SELECT content, role, 1 - (embedding <=> %s::vector) AS similarity
        FROM messages
        ORDER BY embedding <=> %s::vector
        LIMIT %s
    """, (query_embedding, query_embedding, limit))
    return cur.fetchall()
```

content.title: Reranking Systems
content.explanation: Retrieval gets you 100 potentially relevant documents. The LLM's context window fits 5-10. Picking the wrong 5-10 means the model answers with irrelevant or misleading information. Reranking is the critical second stage that takes the initial retrieval results and re-scores them with a more powerful (but slower) model to identify the truly relevant documents. Adding a reranker to your RAG pipeline typically improves answer quality by 10-30%.

content.title: Bi-Encoders vs Cross-Encoders
content.body: Bi-encoders (used for initial retrieval) embed the query and document separately, then compare vectors. They're fast (process millions of documents) but can miss nuanced relevance. Cross-encoders process the query and document together as a single input, using the full attention mechanism to compute a precise relevance score. They're 100x slower but dramatically more accurate. This is why reranking is a two-stage process.

content.title: Cohere Rerank
content.body: The industry-leading reranking API. Send a query + list of documents, receive relevance scores. Simple API call, no infrastructure to manage. Multilingual support. Pricing: per-search (very affordable at most scales). Best for: teams that want the best reranking quality without managing ML infrastructure. Limitation: data is sent to Cohere's servers (privacy concern for some use cases).

content.title: BGE Reranker
content.body: Open-source cross-encoder from BAAI. Available in multiple sizes: `bge-reranker-base` (fast, moderate quality), `bge-reranker-large` (slow, best quality). Fully self-hostable — data never leaves your infrastructure. Run on a single GPU for production throughput. Best for: privacy-sensitive applications and teams that want open-source control over their ranking pipeline.

content.title: ColBERT (Late Interaction)
content.body: A hybrid approach between bi-encoders and cross-encoders. ColBERT computes token-level embeddings for both query and document independently (like a bi-encoder), but scores them using fine-grained token-to-token similarity (like a cross-encoder). This gives 90%+ of cross-encoder quality with 100x the speed. Used by RAGatouille for state-of-the-art efficient reranking.

content.title: Reranking Pipeline Design
content.body:
Standard production pipeline:

1. Retrieve top-50 documents using hybrid search (fast, cheap).
2. Rerank the top-50 using a cross-encoder to get precise relevance scores.
3. Take the top-5 reranked documents.
4. Pass them to the LLM as context. The retrieve-50-rerank-to-5 pattern is the sweet spot between recall (not missing relevant docs) and precision (not including irrelevant ones).

content.title: Reciprocal Reranking
content.body: An advanced technique: after initial reranking, use the LLM itself to re-evaluate the top results. Prompt: 'Given this question and document, rate the relevance from 1-10 and explain why.' This LLM-based reranking is the most expensive but catches subtle relevance signals that embedding-based rerankers miss. Use sparingly — only on the top-3-5 results to control cost.

content.title: Measuring Reranking Impact
content.body:
Before and after adding a reranker, measure:

1. MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) — did the correct document move higher in the results?
2. Recall@K — are more relevant documents in the top-K?
3. Answer quality — use LLM-as-a-Judge to compare RAG answers with and without reranking. A good reranker improves MRR by 15-30% and answer quality by 10-20%.

content.title: Chunking Strategies
content.explanation: Chunking — how you split documents into smaller pieces before embedding — is the most underestimated factor in RAG pipeline quality. Bad chunking creates chunks that are too large (irrelevant information dilutes the embedding), too small (lacking context for the LLM), or split mid-sentence (breaking the semantic meaning). This section covers the spectrum of chunking strategies from simple to sophisticated, with guidance on when to use each.

content.title: Fixed-Size Chunking
content.body: Split text into chunks of exactly N tokens (e.g., 500 tokens per chunk) with an overlap of M tokens (e.g., 50 tokens). The simplest approach — easy to implement, predictable chunk sizes. But it often cuts sentences in half, splitting a concept across two chunks where neither chunk has the full context. Use overlap to mitigate this, but it wastes storage and can confuse retrieval.

content.title: Recursive Character Splitting
content.body:
LangChain's default splitter. Tries to split by paragraphs first (

), then by sentences (.), then by words. This preserves natural document structure better than fixed-size chunking. Parameters: `chunk_size=500, chunk_overlap=50, separators=['

', '
', '.', ' ']`. The recursion means it always tries the most natural boundary first before falling back to smaller units.

content.title: Semantic Chunking
content.body:
Uses an embedding model to detect topic shifts in the text. Process:

1. Embed each sentence.
2. Compare consecutive sentence embeddings.
3. When similarity drops below a threshold (indicating a topic change), insert a chunk boundary. This creates variable-length chunks that align with the document's natural topic structure. More expensive (requires embedding every sentence) but produces significantly better retrieval quality.

content.title: Document-Aware Chunking
content.body: Respect document structure: split by headings (H1, H2, H3), split code files by functions/classes, split legal documents by sections and clauses. This requires a parser that understands the document format (HTML, Markdown, PDF, code). The chunks align with how humans organized the information, which tends to keep related concepts together. Use `MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter` or custom parsers.

content.title: Parent-Child (Small-to-Big) Retrieval
content.body: A two-tier strategy: create small chunks (100-200 tokens) for precise retrieval, but link each small chunk to its parent (the full section or page it came from). During retrieval, search against small chunks for accuracy, but pass the parent document to the LLM for context. This gives you the precision of small chunks with the context richness of large chunks. The best of both worlds.

content.title: Agentic Chunking
content.body: Use an LLM to analyze the document and decide where to place chunk boundaries. Prompt: 'Identify the logical sections in this document and specify where each section starts and ends.' The LLM understands the content semantically and creates chunks that align with the document's conceptual structure. Most expensive approach but produces the highest-quality chunks for complex, unstructured documents.

content.title: Chunk Size Selection Guide
content.body:
The optimal chunk size depends on your embedding model and use case:

1. For models with 512-token context (most bi-encoders): chunks of 200-400 tokens.
2. For models with 8K context (Nomic, Jina): chunks of 500-1000 tokens.
3. For Q&A over technical docs: smaller chunks (200 tokens) for precision.
4. For summarization: larger chunks (500-1000 tokens) for context. Always evaluate: try 3-4 chunk sizes and measure retrieval quality on your specific dataset.

```python
text = """Chapter 1: Introduction to AI
Artificial intelligence is a broad field...

Chapter 2: Machine Learning

chunks = splitter.split_text(text)

for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
```
